You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in ANKAASE, a small community tucked in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District of the Central Region. I was born and raised here; our whole village barely clocks 318 people, so everyone knows everyone — their children, their jokes, the times they shout for help. I’m 24 now. I finished Senior Secondary School and then, like a lot of young men here, I looked for steady work rather than more school. On 9 February 2022 I started a full-time job that helped settle things at home and gave me a clearer rhythm to my days.

My household is four people aside from me: my mother, my father and my younger sister. We live in a modest compound house with a small front yard where the roosters announce the sunrise. My parents taught me to take responsibility early. Even now, after getting employed, much of what I earn goes to keeping the household running — food is the biggest expense. We spend about 200 Ghanaian cedis a week on food: fresh plantain, rice, gari, groundnuts, some fish when we can, and the occasional treat. Non-food bills are tight but manageable — about 10 cedis a week for things like water and top-ups. All things considered, I’d say our economic condition is good; we don’t have luxuries, but we don’t panic over small emergencies either.

Work takes up most of my weekdays. I commute from ANKAASE to the workplace; sometimes I walk to the main road to catch a trotro or hop a motorbike if I’m in a hurry. The things that keep me steady — the predictable paycheck, the camaraderie with colleagues, the small pride of contributing to my family — matter more than the job title itself. Having a registered mobile number has been a small but important asset: I can get calls about shifts, receive money transfers, and stay in touch with suppliers and friends. I don’t take it for granted — a good network connection can solve a lot of problems.

Health is something I think about practically. The nearest health clinic is a little over four kilometers from where we live — 4.356 kilometers, to be exact. That distance matters when someone has a fever in the night or when a child needs vaccination. We make the trip when necessary; it’s not far, but for an older relative or a sick child it can feel long, and transportation isn’t always immediately available. That reality made my decision about COVID-19 vaccines straightforward: I want to protect myself and my family, and I trust the clinic staff when they recommend vaccination. If vaccines are available to me, I would get the first shot within the first six weeks — no hesitation. To me, it’s common sense and communal responsibility; if I protect myself, I protect the people I live with and the neighbors I share the market with.

Life here moves with the seasons. There are market days when the road hums with traders and buses; there are quieter afternoons when the kids play football under the shade of the mango tree. My education at SSS taught me to read and to think ahead; my work taught me discipline; home taught me loyalty. I don’t see myself staying in the village forever — I’d like to learn new skills and maybe start a small business one day — but ANKAASE will always be the place that shaped me.

I am an 18-year-old woman from Amoanda, a small community in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District of the Central Region. I finished Senior Secondary School not long ago and came home hopeful that I would find work or an apprenticeship quickly, but things have been slow. Our village is close-knit — about 3,455 people live here — and everyone knows each other’s struggles and small victories. At home there are four other people besides me, so five of us share what little we have. We live simply, and every cedi has to stretch. On average our household spends about 35 Ghanaian cedis a week on food, and even that sometimes feels like too little. My parents and younger siblings depend on me to help however I can.

Daily life here is a mixture of small chores, long walks, and waiting for chances. I wake early to help with sweeping and fetching water, then I try to look for casual work or help friends and relatives with farming or small trading. I don’t have a steady job at the moment — I am unemployed — so my hours are a patchwork of favors and temporary tasks. When I was in school I dreamed of training to be a nurse or a teacher, but with our current finances — I would describe our household’s overall economic condition as bad — those plans are on hold until something changes.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I was born and raised in Kwabea Mampong, a small village in the Upper Manya Krobo District, and I have lived here my whole life. I am 65 years old now, a man who finished middle school and then learned the work of the land and the market with my own hands. For most of my life I labored as a smallholder farmer, growing maize and cassava, and selling a little when the harvest was good. I retired from active farming some years ago, though I still help when I can and take care of small errands around the compound.

Our village is small — only about 215 people — and everyone more or less knows everyone else. There is a quiet rhythm to life here: mornings begin with the sound of roosters and the smoke from pots being lit for porridge; afternoons are for work, mending, and sometimes visiting the nearby neighbors; evenings bring the women together by the well and the men sharing stories under the mango tree. I live in a compound with three other people who rely on me: my wife and two grandchildren who are staying with us while their parents try to find work in a town farther away. They keep me busy and give me purpose.

Money is always on my mind. Each week our household spends about 60 Ghanaian Cedis on food — yam, gari, rice, a little palm oil and vegetables — and about 80 cedis on non-food items like water, electricity when we can pay it, rent for a small room where my grandchildren sleep, and school fees for the younger one. I try to stretch every cedi, but the truth is our situation is bad. There are days when I count coins and still worry how we will meet the next week’s expenses. My pension, when it comes, is small and irregular, and most of my income now comes from selling a little produce or small odd jobs in the community.

Access to services is a challenge. The nearest health clinic is not nearby — it sits roughly 7.7 kilometers away. If someone is sick we either hire a motorbike or walk, and the cost and time involved often keep people from going until illnesses get worse. I do not have a registered mobile number where I can receive payments; I never got into using mobile money and find it difficult without trust or a reliable phone. That isolation makes it harder to get news or help when it is needed.

I have strong ties to our community — I take part in funerals, help when a neighbor needs a hand, and sometimes attend the small gatherings at the church. I am proud of my family and the life we have carved out, but I worry about the future of my grandchildren and how they will find steady work or education.

When it comes to the new things the world brings, like the COVID-19 vaccine, I am cautious. If you asked me whether I would take a first shot within the first six weeks after it became available to me, I would say there is only about an 18% chance. I worry about the side effects, I have heard stories that worry me, and the journey to the clinic would be another barrier. If the health workers came to our village, explained clearly, and there was support to get to the clinic, I might change my mind — but as things stand I remain hesitant.

This is my life in Kwabea Mampong: a simple, steady existence shaped by work, family, small comforts, and the daily struggle to make ends meet while holding on to the dignity of being an elder in my community.

I am 34 years old and I live in Asempanaye, a small but busy community in the Assin North District of the Central Region. Our village is not very big — about 3,838 people — so everybody knows somebody, and life moves at a familiar, neighborly pace.

I finished JSS/JHS when I was a teenager. School was important to my parents, but we didn’t have the money or the opportunities for me to go further. After JHS I stayed home, helped my mother and later started caring for my own family. I am not currently employed outside the home; most days my work is managing the household and looking after our children. There are six other people living in our house with me right now — between my partner, my in-laws, and our relatives — and three children under 18 who depend on me for nearly everything. My days begin early: fetching water when needed, preparing meals, sweeping, washing clothes, and making sure the children get ready for school. When there’s time, I help with small jobs around the compound or with a neighbor’s farm to earn a little extra.

Money is tight in some ways but, all things considered, I would say our household’s financial condition is very good. My husband — or a relative who helps support us — has steady work that brings in enough income so we can live comfortably. We spend about 120 Ghanaian cedis a week on food; that covers rice, gari, plantain, fish, vegetables and the children’s school snacks. On non-food items like water, electricity, rent and school supplies we spend around 35 cedis a week. We budget carefully, and because several adults contribute, we manage to save small amounts now and then for bigger needs.

One convenience I appreciate is how close the health clinic is — less than a kilometer away, about 0.72 km. If one of the children gets a fever or someone needs antenatal care, the clinic is easy to reach. I have a registered mobile number, which I use to keep in touch with family, receive news, and sometimes to receive mobile money transfers. It helps a lot, especially when coordinating school fees or when my partner is working away and needs to send money.

I want to protect my family, but I am worried about possible side effects and I have seen different stories and opinions from people in the community. I would need to see trusted health workers explain clearly how safe it is and what the benefits are before I go quickly to get vaccinated. Until then I am careful — I encourage handwashing, keep our space clean, and try to teach the children good habits.

Life here is rooted in family and routine. I take pride in caring for our home and children, and I hope to find small ways to contribute more financially in the future — maybe by starting a small trading business or joining a women’s group. For now, I focus on keeping our household stable, supporting the children’s education, and making sure that, despite limited formal schooling, we give them a chance to go further than I did.

After JHS I stayed home, helped my mother and later started caring for my own family. I am not currently employed outside the home; most days my work is managing the household and looking after our children. I am forty-six years old and I live in Ayaase, a small community in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central region. I remember the exact morning the interviewer came — 14 February 2022 at 08:17 — because it felt like one of those days when the questions you are asked force you to think about everything you have been holding together for years. Ayaase is small; about one thousand five hundred and eighty-one people live here. We all know one another by sight and by the stories our parents told, but life is still full of hard choices.

I only completed primary school. There were no funds to continue after that, so I went straight to work. I have been employed full time for many years now; most days I wake before dawn to prepare food and goods for the local market, or I go out to help on a nearby farm for a wage. My work is honest and it keeps food on the table, but it is physical and the pay is limited. At home we are six people altogether — that’s me plus five others — and two of those are children under eighteen. The children are the reason I keep going. They need schoolbooks, uniforms, and sometimes money for small things, and that responsibility sits heavy on me.

Money is tight. On average we spend about 200 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food — rice, gari, plantain, tomatoes, the staples that keep us fed — and another 40 cedis on non-food essentials like electricity tokens, water, and the occasional school fee. Despite those outlays, I would describe our household’s condition as bad. There are days I lie awake thinking about unexpected expenses: a sudden illness, a pestilence in the farm, or when a child needs new shoes. The nearest health clinic is not close — it’s roughly 9.55 kilometers from my house. That distance means a long walk or a costly motorbike ride which we cannot always afford. I have a mobile number registered so people can call me, and I use it for important calls and to arrange transport when needed, but I do not use social media at all; I have never been on Facebook or WhatsApp. News comes to me through neighbors, radio, or word of mouth.

Community is everything here. I maintain friendships beyond my village; I have about twenty-five friends and acquaintances in another village where I trade and sometimes help with seasonal work. They are my safety net — someone to lend a little cash in a pinch, to trade goods with, or to share news about jobs and prices. We rely on each other for barter and favors, and the ties between villages are a practical lifeline as much as they are social ones.

When the conversation turned to health and vaccines during the interview, I surprised even myself — I said there was an eighty-two percent chance I would take a first COVID-19 vaccine within the first six weeks it became available to me. I do not keep up with online arguments or rumors; my choice comes from something simpler: a wish to protect my children and the older people in the house, and a trust in the nurses I have known for years at outreach days. There is caution, sure — we have seen things in the world and heard stories — but the fear of sickness and losing what little we have is stronger.

Some days I am hopeful. I try to save a little from what I earn, though it is rarely more than a few cedis. I dream of a small, sturdier house with fewer leaks, of a child finishing school and finding work that does not wear them down so early. Other days I am exhausted by the routine and by how slowly things seem to change. Still, I rise with the sun, prepare the day’s work, tend to my family, and hold tight to the small friendships and practical choices that keep us moving forward.

Some days I am hopeful. I try to save a little from what I earn, though it is rarely more than a few cedis. I dream of a small, sturdier house with fewer leaks, of a child finishing school and finding work that does not wear them down so early. Other days I am exhausted by the routine and by how slowly things seem to change. Still, I rise with the sun, prepare the day’s work, tend to my family, and hold tight to the small friendships and practical choices that keep us moving forward.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in a small place called Pewodie, a tight cluster of houses where everybody knows everybody and the whole village counts fewer than three hundred people. I was born and raised here in the Central Region, in the Assin North District, and even now at 35 I still wake to the same sounds I heard as a child — roosters, distant motors, and neighbors calling to one another. I finished Senior High School and that education has shaped how I move through life: it opened a few doors, but it didn’t take me away from home the way university might have.

On 18 February 2022 I took part in a study and answered some questions about my life. I work full time to support a household of five — me plus four others — and our life is a balancing act. My wife and I have one child under eighteen, a lively little boy who fills our house with noise and homework. The other two people living with us are my mother and my younger sister; we look after each other. We spend about 150 cedis a week on food — enough for staples, ground provisions, fish or meat a few times in the week, and a few treats for the boy when we can manage. On good weeks we feel comfortable; on many weeks I would describe our situation as neither good nor bad — stable, but always with an eye on the bills.

My work keeps me busy. I’m employed full time in the nearby town — some days I go into town by trotro, other days I take my motorbike. My job gives a steady income and some routine; it also means I’m often on the road, running errands after work, buying supplies, and making sure the household is sorted. Living in a small community means services are not always close: the nearest health clinic is about 7.5 kilometers away. That distance matters — when someone is sick you have to organize transport or borrow money, and it makes routine trips for prevention and vaccination a bigger decision than they would be in a town.

I carry a registered mobile number and it is central to how I keep things together. I call my boss, check messages about market prices, share pictures of my son with family, and get updates from friends. The phone is also how I hear news about health campaigns like the COVID-19 vaccine. When asked whether I would take a first vaccine shot within the first six weeks after it became available to me, I answered honestly that my chances were around forty percent. I am not completely against it — I see the benefit — but I worry about side effects, I worry about losing a day’s pay if I feel unwell afterward, and the clinic’s distance makes the logistics harder. I’m the kind of person who wants to be sure before committing.

Life here moves at a steady pace. Mornings start early with market runs or farm tasks, afternoons are for work and repairs around the compound, evenings for cooking and helping my son with schoolwork by candle or the small generator when the light is out. We attend church and community meetings; we help neighbors and they help us. I am proud of what we have built together, even when the money is tight and the clinic feels too far away. I am careful with what I spend, I keep open lines with my family through my phone, and I make decisions not just for myself but for the people depending on me. That is the story of my life in Pewodie up to and beyond that February morning in 2022.

I am 35 years old, and on the morning of 2022-02-16 at 04:13 I sat with an interviewer and answered questions about my life — a moment that made me pause and reflect on how I arrived where I am. I grew up in the Central Region and I still live in the small community of ZAMBOREE in the Assin North District. Our village is tiny — only 128 people — so everyone knows everyone, and life here moves at a steady, familiar pace.

I finished senior high school (SSS/SHS), and that education has served me well. With that background I found steady, full-time work that allows me to support my family comfortably. I live in a household with four other people — my partner and our three children, who are all under 18. Mornings in our house are busy: getting the children ready for school, preparing breakfast, and making sure everyone has what they need before I leave for work. Because I work full time, my daily routine is about balancing responsibility at my job with responsibility at home.

Money matters are important to me, but we are fortunate. We spend about 210 Ghanaian cedis a week on food, and I would describe our household’s economic situation as “very good.” That doesn’t mean life is without challenges, but it does mean we rarely worry about basic needs. We use my registered mobile number daily — to keep in touch with family, to handle transactions, and to coordinate the children’s activities and medical appointments.

Access to health care is something I pay attention to because of my children. The nearest health clinic is not right next door — it is about 9.490954451 kilometers away. That distance matters when a child is sick or requires routine care; we plan and combine trips when we can. The clinic is far enough that you learn to be prepared at home, but close enough that we can get help when we need it.

My work gives me stability and a sense of purpose. I am proud to provide for my family and to watch my children grow and learn. Living in a small community like ZAMBOREE means our neighbors are part of our extended family. We help each other with childcare, share produce when the harvest is good, and gather for important events. The closeness of the village keeps us connected and grounded.

When COVID-19 vaccines became available, I was ready to take the first dose as soon as I could — I believed in protecting myself, my children, and the wider community. If I had to give a number, my chance of taking the first shot within the first six weeks of availability was 100%. For me, vaccination was a responsible step to keep my household healthy and to maintain the stability we had worked hard to build.

This is my life in ZAMBOREE: practical, busy, and anchored by family and community. I am a woman who finished senior high, works full time, manages a household of five, and keeps a close eye on health and finances so that our small family can thrive in our little village.

Our village is small—about seven hundred and six people—and everyone knows each other. Life here moves with the seasons: planting, fishing, buying and selling what we can, and relying on one another when things get hard.

I woke up before dawn on 25 February 2022 — the clock on my phone read 05:03 when I finished answering the first questions for that survey. That small moment caught me thinking about how my life has arranged itself so far: 25 years old, born and raised in Sawa, a close-knit community in the Upper Manya Krobo District of the Eastern Region. People here call me steady; I call myself someone still learning how to balance responsibility and hope.

I grew up in a house that now holds just one other person besides me — my mother. We’ve always been two in the household for as long as I can remember. After my father passed away when I was young, my mother worked tirelessly to keep us afloat. She sells produce and sometimes helps with a neighbor’s shea processing. That steady income is one reason I feel comfortable describing our economic situation as “very good.” It’s relative: we don’t have much in the way of luxury, but we have enough food each week, a small plot of land that yields some crops, and people in the community who watch out for us.

I finished JSS/JHS, and those lessons still shape me. I remember the schoolhouse — the chalk dust, the reed fences, the afternoons when we’d race home because there was something to be harvested or a baby goat that needed tying up. Completing JHS felt like an achievement then, but I also felt the tug of wanting more. Right now I’m a student again, returning to learning in a different way — attending a vocational program a few towns away and taking some evening classes through a distance program when I can. Some days I’m on the motorbike to classes, other times I study by lantern if the electricity is out. Education at my level taught me to be practical, to value skills you can use tomorrow, and to keep an ear open for whoever needs help in the village.

We live in a village of about 731 people. That number gives Sawa a rhythm that is intimate but not claustrophobic — everyone knows most people, but there’s always someone new moving through. My nearest neighbors are more than friends; they’re almost family. Locally I have about four people I count as my closest network — two neighbors, an uncle who lives three compounds down, and a teacher who still gives me advice. These are the ones I can call on after dusk if something goes wrong. Beyond the village, I’ve kept ties with about ten friends and acquaintances in another nearby village. We trade stories, labor, and sometimes produce; when there’s a funeral or a celebration, it’s those cross-village connections that often make things possible.

Health care is practical and a little distant. The nearest clinic is 3.212 kilometers from my home — far enough that a run-in with fever or a complicated illness becomes something we plan for. If it’s a minor thing we walk, but for anything urgent we find transport or arrange for a motorbike. That distance has shaped how my family treats minor ailments: prevention, herbal remedies, and careful watching. When the COVID-19 vaccines started to roll out, I was cautious. On that morning in late February I told the interviewer I thought there was a 50 percent chance I’d take a first shot within six weeks of availability. That answer came from a place of balance: I worry about side effects and prefer to see how things go, but I also trust the health workers and want to protect my mother and the people I care about.

Money matters in predictable ways. Our household spends about 140 Ghanaian cedis a week on food and about 10 cedis on non-food expenses like water or small school fees. Those numbers don’t make us wealthy, but they do buy staples, occasional fish or meat, and a little school material for my ongoing studies. We budget carefully; my mother is a master at it. When I can, I chip in with odd jobs — helping farmers during harvest, carrying goods for traders, or tutoring younger children in reading and arithmetic. I keep the ledgers in my head and in a small notebook; we’re careful savers and have enough that I can honestly say our household’s economic condition is very good compared with where we started. I remember the morning I filled out that interview questionnaire — 13 February 2022 — sitting on the wooden bench under the neem tree in front of our compound in Mokwa. I was 31 then, and the sun had just warmed the red earth. My name is common here, but what matters more to me is the life I’ve built in this small village of about 1,176 people in Twifo Atti Morkwa District, Central Region. Everyone knows each other by sight; a nod at the market, a greeting at the clinic, and the day moves on.

I finished Senior High School back home and, like many of us, settled into work that could support a young family. I’m employed full time at the local cocoa buying center — mostly supervising weigh-ins, keeping records, and helping coordinate deliveries to the town. It’s honest work and steady; I start early when the mist is still on the cocoa farms and finish when the afternoon heat settles. My education at SSS/SHS taught me enough to read contracts and balance accounts, and over time I learned the practical side of the trade from older hands in the community.

At home I live with three people aside from myself — my wife and our two small children. Our compound is modest: a compound house with a front porch where my wife hangs laundry and where the children chase lizards in the dust. We live close to the clinic — only about 0.315 kilometers away — which I thank the ancestors for every time one of the kids gets a fever. That short walk to the clinic gives me peace of mind; when my youngest had a bad cough last wet season, we were in and out with advice and medicine before the cough turned to something worse.

Money moves through our household in tight cycles. On average we spend about 450 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food — staple fufu, plantain, gari, rice, fresh fish when we can, and the small treats for the children. Food is priority; we eat well when the harvests are good and draw in when they’re not. Non-food expenses are about 80 cedis a week — electricity, water, a bit toward rent of the room we keep for visiting family, and small school fees for the children. That number doesn’t sound large when you say it, but stretched over a month it covers a lot of small needs: a uniform, kerosene, charging the phone, or the occasional hospital bill. If someone asks how we are doing, I say “neither good nor bad” — it’s honest. We are stable enough to sleep at night, but there’s always a little worry about the next leak, the next medical bill, or the season.

My phone is always with me — I have a registered mobile number. It’s how I get paid sometimes, how I send money home to my wife when I’m out on a trip, and how I get messages from the clinic about health campaigns or cocoa prices. Mobile money and WhatsApp groups have become the lifeblood of business and family life here. I use the same number to call my father in the regional capital and to receive notifications about community meetings or vaccination drives.

When it comes to health decisions, I’m careful. The pandemic changed how we all think about being responsible — not just for ourselves but for our families and neighbors. If a vaccine becomes available to me, I’m about 97 percent certain I’ll take the first shot within six weeks. That’s not fear; it’s duty. The clinic is close, the nurses are people I know, and I’ve seen campaigns at the marketplace explaining the benefits. I don’t want to be the reason my wife or the children fall sick. I’ve had vaccinations before; it’s just another step to protect the people who depend on me.

Life in Mokwa moves with the seasons: planting, harvest, market days, and the occasional funeral that brings everyone together. I find pride in the routine — in keeping the books at work, in making sure my children have school uniforms, in the small flourishes like buying oranges when they’re in season. I’m not wealthy, but I’ve built a life that’s steady, connected, and responsible. I remember the morning I filled out that interview questionnaire — 13 February 2022 — sitting on the wooden bench under the neem tree in front of our compound in Mokwa. I was 31 then, and the sun had just warmed the red earth. My name is common here, but what matters more to me is the life I’ve built in this small village of about 1,176 people in Twifo Atti Morkwa District, Central Region. Everyone knows each other by sight; a nod at the market, a greeting at the clinic, and the day moves on.

I finished Senior High School back home and, like many of us, settled into work that could support a young family. I’m employed full time at the local cocoa buying center — mostly supervising weigh-ins, keeping records, and helping coordinate deliveries to the town. It’s honest work and steady; I start early when the mist is still on the cocoa farms and finish when the afternoon heat settles. My education at SSS/SHS taught me enough to read contracts and balance accounts, and over time I learned the practical side of the trade from older hands in the community.

At home I live with three people aside from myself — my wife and our two small children. Our compound is modest: a compound house with a front porch where my wife hangs laundry and where the children chase lizards in the dust. We live close to the clinic — only about 0.315 kilometers away — which I thank the ancestors for every time one of the kids gets a fever. That short walk to the clinic gives me peace of mind; when my youngest had a bad cough last wet season, we were in and out with advice and medicine before the cough turned to something worse.

Money moves through our household in tight cycles. On average we spend about 450 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food — staple fufu, plantain, gari, rice, fresh fish when we can, and the small treats for the children. Food is priority; we eat well when the harvests are good and draw in when they’re not. Non-food expenses are about 80 cedis a week — electricity, water, a bit toward rent of the room we keep for visiting family, and small school fees for the children. That number doesn’t sound large when you say it, but stretched over a month it covers a lot of small needs: a uniform, kerosene, charging the phone, or the occasional hospital bill. If someone asks how we are doing, I say “neither good nor bad” — it’s honest. We are stable enough to sleep at night, but there’s always a little worry about the next leak, the next medical bill, or the season.

My phone is always with me — I have a registered mobile number. It’s how I get paid sometimes, how I send money home to my wife when I’m out on a trip, and how I get messages from the clinic about health campaigns or cocoa prices. Mobile money and WhatsApp groups have become the lifeblood of business and family life here. I use the same number to call my father in the regional capital and to receive notifications about community meetings or vaccination drives.

When it comes to health decisions, I’m careful. The pandemic changed how we all think about being responsible — not just for ourselves but for our families and neighbors. If a vaccine becomes available to me, I’m about 97 percent certain I’ll take the first shot within six weeks. That’s not fear; it’s duty. The clinic is close, the nurses are people I know, and I’ve seen campaigns at the marketplace explaining the benefits. I don’t want to be the reason my wife or the children fall sick. I’ve had vaccinations before; it’s just another step to protect the people who depend on me.

Life in Mokwa moves with the seasons: planting, harvest, market days, and the occasional funeral that brings everyone together. I find pride in the routine — in keeping the books at work, in making sure my children have school uniforms, in the small flourishes like buying oranges when they’re in season. I’m not wealthy, but I’ve built a life that’s steady, connected, and responsible. That’s enough for now — and when the next challenge comes, whether a drought or a health scare, I know where to start: at the clinic down the road, with my family at my back, and my phone in my hand.

I was born and raised in this part of the Eastern Region, and I still live in Kwabea Mampong in the Upper Manya Krobo District. I finished only primary school, but I learned early to get my hands dirty and to work hard for my family. On 26 February 2022, at 02:31 in the morning — a time I remember because it was when I started my current full‑time job — my life settled into a steadier rhythm. The work isn’t fancy, but it pays the bills and keeps food on the table for the seven of us who share the compound.

My house is full most of the time: six people live with me besides myself, and four of those are children under eighteen. Mornings begin before dawn. I check the small store of food I keep for the household, load what we need for the market when necessary, and set off to the depot where I work as a storekeeper and occasional buyer of produce. The depot connects farmers in this district, and because I handle goods every day I have been able to keep a steady income that lets me provide well for my family. I know the weight of every bag of maize, cassava, or plantain that passes through my hands, and I take pride in making sure nothing goes to waste.

We live in a village of about 215 people — small enough that everyone knows each other’s name, but large enough that there’s always someone to talk to when the evening comes. We don’t use social media; I’ve never cared for it. My phone is for calls and messages only; I have a registered number and I use it to coordinate business, call relatives in other places, and check in with the children’s school when needed. Most of my social life is face to face. I can count on three people nearby who are part of my close social network — neighbors I grew up with and friends who have been through the same seasons of planting and harvest with me. I also have four family members who live in another village and one friend in a different village; when things are difficult we help each other across those distances.

Money can be a worry in rural life, but I am careful and fortunate enough that I rate our household’s condition as “very good.” That is because I prioritize food — we spend about 360 Ghanaian Cedis on food each week. With four growing children and other adults in the household, that food budget is necessary; there are many mouths to feed and I make sure there is always enough of the staples and sometimes a little extra for fish or meat when business is good. We spend very little on non‑food items each week — around 10 cedis — because we own our home and utilities are minimal; rent and large bills are not a regular burden here.

Living in a rural area means some challenges: the nearest health clinic is nearly 7.8 kilometers away. When a child falls sick, I prepare for the walk or arrange transport; those are always anxious hours. Still, the village’s closeness creates a kind of security — if someone needs help carrying a sick child to the road or lending a little money, neighbors step in.

Because I only had a primary education, I’ve always placed a different kind of value on learning — not just academic, but practical skills, honesty, and persistence. I want more for my children. I worry about school fees and the cost of secondary education, but I also see them eager and bright, and that keeps me going. My work provides a stable income and, more importantly, a routine. I wake early, move goods, talk to farmers, bargain when necessary, and make sure my family’s needs are met before I rest.

Evenings are for the family: we eat together, share news from the day, and the children practice reading or finish chores. I am proud we have kept such a steady household. I do not crave the trappings of big towns; I value the quiet here and the sense that my labor directly supports my children’s plates and their future. My network may be small, my schooling modest, and my phone only for calls, but what I have built in Kwabea Mampong is enough to make me feel steady and hopeful for the years to come.

I was born and raised in this part of the Eastern Region, and I still live in Kwabea Mampong in the Upper Manya Krobo District. I finished only primary school, but I learned early to get my hands dirty and to work hard for my family. On 26 February 2022, at 02:31 in the morning — a time I remember because it was when I started my current full‑time job — my life settled into a steadier rhythm. The work isn’t fancy, but it pays the bills and keeps food on the table for the seven of us who share the compound.

My house is full most of the time: six people live with me besides myself, and four of those are children under eighteen. Mornings begin before dawn. I check the small store of food I keep for the household, load what we need for the market when necessary, and set off to the depot where I work as a storekeeper and occasional buyer of produce. The depot connects farmers in this district, and because I handle goods every day I have been able to keep a steady income that lets me provide well for my family. I know the weight of every bag of maize, cassava, or plantain that passes through my hands, and I take pride in making sure nothing goes to waste.

We live in a village of about 215 people — small enough that everyone knows each other’s name, but large enough that there’s always someone to talk to when the evening comes. We don’t use social media; I’ve never cared for it. My phone is for calls and messages only; I have a registered number and I use it to coordinate business, call relatives in other places, and check in with the children’s school when needed. Most of my social life is face to face. I can count on three people nearby who are part of my close social network — neighbors I grew up with and friends who have been through the same seasons of planting and harvest with me. I also have four family members who live in another village and one friend in a different village; when things are difficult we help each other across those distances.

Money can be a worry in rural life, but I am careful and fortunate enough that I rate our household’s condition as “very good.” That is because I prioritize food — we spend about 360 Ghanaian Cedis on food each week. With four growing children and other adults in the household, that food budget is necessary; there are many mouths to feed and I make sure there is always enough of the staples and sometimes a little extra for fish or meat when business is good. We spend very little on non‑food items each week — around 10 cedis — because we own our home and utilities are minimal; rent and large bills are not a regular burden here.

Living in a rural area means some challenges: the nearest health clinic is nearly 7.8 kilometers away. When a child falls sick, I prepare for the walk or arrange transport; those are always anxious hours. Still, the village’s closeness creates a kind of security — if someone needs help carrying a sick child to the road or lending a little money, neighbors step in.

Because I only had a primary education, I’ve always placed a different kind of value on learning — not just academic, but practical skills, honesty, and persistence. I want more for my children. I worry about school fees and the cost of secondary education, but I also see them eager and bright, and that keeps me going. My work provides a stable income and, more importantly, a routine. I wake early, move goods, talk to farmers, bargain when necessary, and make sure my family’s needs are met before I rest.

Evenings are for the family: we eat together, share news from the day, and the children practice reading or finish chores. I am proud we have kept such a steady household. I do not crave the trappings of big towns; I value the quiet here and the sense that my labor directly supports my children’s plates and their future. My network may be small, my schooling modest, and my phone only for calls, but what I have built in Kwabea Mampong is enough to make me feel steady and hopeful for the years to come.

I started this study on 2022-02-09 at 05:05, and I remember answering each question thinking about the small rhythms of life in Kwekuboa.

I am 27 years old and I grew up here in the Central Region, in the Asikuma Odoben Brankwa District. Our village is small—about 610 people—and everyone knows one another. I only completed primary school, but I learned many practical things from my mother and neighbours, and I am proud of the life I have built with what I know.

I work full time as a market vendor in the nearby town, selling a mix of foodstuffs and cooked meals. My days begin early: I wake before sunrise to prepare food and pack produce, walk or take a trotro to the market, and stay there until late afternoon. The work is tiring but steady, and it brings in enough for my household to be comfortable. At home we are six people in total: five people live with me besides myself. Two children under eighteen live with us—my little ones, a six-year-old and a three-year-old—who keep the house lively and make everything I do feel important. The others in the household include my husband and my mother-in-law; sometimes my younger brother stays with us as well when he needs help. We share chores and meals, and decision-making is something we do together.

On average we spend about 150 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food. Because we feed a full house and I also sell some cooked food at the market, groceries and ingredients are our biggest expense. For non-food items—electricity, water, small fees—we spend around 20 Cedis a week. Even with the limited formal education I received, I have learned to budget carefully. Right now I would describe our household’s economic condition as good: we are able to meet our needs, pay for the children’s small school expenses, and keep a little aside for emergencies.

One of the practical difficulties of living in Kwekuboa is the distance to medical services. The nearest health clinic is almost 4.9 kilometres away. When one of the children needs care or when someone in the household is unwell, I either borrow a motorbike ride or walk if the situation allows. The journey can be hard in the rainy season, so I take prevention seriously and try to keep everyone healthy.

I have a registered mobile number that I use every day. It helps me keep in touch with family and customers, receive orders, and use mobile money for transactions—very useful for business and managing household money. Because I hear news and health information through my phone and from the clinic when I visit, I was certain about the COVID-19 vaccine. If it becomes available to me, I’m 100% sure I will get the first shot within the first six weeks. I want to protect my children and my family, and I trust what the health workers tell us.

My life here is simple but full. I take pride in my work, in being able to support my family, and in the little community we have in Kwekuboa. I may only have primary education, but I manage our household finances, run my stall, and plan for the children’s future. I hope to keep building a stable life for them so they have more choices than I did.

I live in Junction — we call it Atu-Dawda — a small, lively community in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District of the Central Region. On the morning of 10 February 2022 at 8:12 I sat down to answer an interview about my life; thinking about those questions made me reflect on how I got here and what matters most to me now.

I am 36 years old. I finished junior high school (JSS/JHS), and although I didn’t continue to senior high, the years in school taught me to read, write and manage numbers well enough to run a household and hold a steady job. I work full time in a small enterprise in the nearby town — I handle administrative tasks, cash handling and customer relations. It is not glamorous, but it is steady and it allows me to provide for my family and save a little each month.

Our village is small by some standards — about 1,578 people live here — and everyone knows most everyone else. Mornings usually begin with the sound of cockcrow, children getting ready for school, and women heading to the market with bundles of cassava, plantain or tomatoes. I live in a house with five other people besides me. We are a household of six: my husband, my three children who are all under eighteen, and my mother-in-law who helps with the cooking and childcare when I have to work late. The house is full most of the time, sometimes loud, but always warm.

Money is a daily balancing act. On average we spend about 170 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. That covers staples, the children’s meals, and the occasional treat. Non-food expenses — electricity, water, small school fees or transport — amount to about 10 cedis a week most of the time because some bills are infrequent or paid in larger sums monthly. Overall, I would rate our household’s financial situation as good. We are not wealthy by any measure, but with steady work, help from family, and careful planning, we have what we need. I try to budget so that the children have shoes for school, and so I can save toward sending them further in education than I went.

Health care is something I think about, especially with three growing children. The nearest health clinic is about 5.3 kilometers from our home. It is not right next door, but it is reachable — a motorbike ride if we have money, or a long walk when we do not. I keep the clinic in mind when we have fevers, vaccinations or when a child needs a prescription. I have a registered mobile number that I use for calls, for mobile money, and to stay informed: the clinic sometimes sends messages about outreach days or vaccination drives, and the number helps me coordinate transport or ask for help when needed.

Community life here revolves around work and faith. On market days the main road fills with traders selling pepper, fish, yams and clothes. We attend church and small community meetings; my mother-in-law often leads a cooking group that makes soups for funerals or special occasions. I try to be present — I want my children to see responsibility and community service modeled for them.

Education for the children is a priority I take seriously. I did what I could with my JSS education, and I hope they will have opportunities to go further. At home I help with homework the best I can, and we encourage reading. I remind them that school is their way out of hard, physically demanding work and into more choices.

About the COVID-19 vaccine: when asked how likely I was to take the first shot within the first six weeks of availability, I said 74 percent. I am leaning toward getting vaccinated fairly quickly because I want to protect my family and because my job brings me into contact with many people. Still, I have questions about safety and timing, and I want to be reassured by trustworthy health workers. The clinic’s outreach messages on my phone help, and so do conversations with neighbors who have been vaccinated.

Day-to-day life is busy but purposeful. I wake early, prepare breakfast for the children, check messages on my phone, and then head to work. Afternoons might be spent at the market or helping at the local community center. Evenings are for homework, cooking, and talking about the day. I tighten the household budget where I can, and I save small amounts so that when school fees or emergencies come, we are ready.

Looking ahead, my hope is simple: that my children will have choices I didn’t, that we maintain our good household condition, and that the community continues to grow with better health and education services closer to home. I am proud of what we have managed so far, and I keep working — for stability, for my children, and for the quiet peace of knowing we will be alright.

When I was a young man I learned many practical things by doing. I started helping older neighbors with fishing and small-scale trade and later found a steady full-time job in Akosombo. I have worked there for many years and that steady income has kept my family comfortable. We spend about 280 Ghanaian cedis a week on food and another 70 cedis on non-food needs like electricity, water and school contributions. People around here might be surprised to hear that — by local standards our household’s financial situation is very good, and I try to manage what I earn so we can stay that way.

At home I live with two others — my wife and one of my children who still depends on us. I have other family scattered across villages: eight of my relatives live in another village, and there are about twelve friends and acquaintances I know who live outside Opokuase. Rumors travel fast in person, and sometimes that creates doubts. I prefer to wait a little, ask questions, and decide based on what I learn from neighbors and the clinic.

I do not use social media at all. My phone is for calls and messages — to check on my children, to speak with relatives in other villages, and to arrange business. I value face-to-face conversations; they are how we resolve misunderstandings and make plans. When I need new ideas about farming, trading, or health, I go to trusted elders, colleagues, or the extension officer when they visit.

I hope the children will have more schooling than I did. For myself, I want to keep working, keep the household comfortable, and be there for my people when they need me.

My schooling stopped after primary level — there wasn’t much money, and my parents needed hands in the fields and at the market more than they needed another student. Still, the little I learned at primary school has helped me all my life: reading notices, doing basic sums for my stall and household accounts, and filling in forms when I need to.

When I was a young man I learned many practical things by doing. I started helping older neighbors with fishing and small-scale trade and later found a steady full-time job in Akosombo. I have worked there for many years and that steady income has kept my family comfortable. We spend about 280 Ghanaian cedis a week on food and another 70 cedis on non-food needs like electricity, water and school contributions. People around here might be surprised to hear that — by local standards our household’s financial situation is very good, and I try to manage what I earn so we can stay that way.

I do not use social media, so my information comes from people I trust in the village, the radio if there is a clear announcement, and the health workers when they visit. I worry about the small things — whether the roof will need repairs, whether school fees will arrive on time for the young ones, whether my mother in the other village is getting enough help — but I also enjoy the good parts: the smell of fresh tilapia in the market on market day, the rhythm of work at the plant, and the evenings when the family sits together and shares a meal. I grew up in Asesewa Community D, a small place in the Upper Manya Krobo District of the Eastern Region where everyone knows everyone and the rhythm of life follows market days and harvests. I am 18 now, but I still remember the narrow dirt roads, the red dust that sticks to your feet in the dry season, and the evening hum of people sitting outside their compound walls telling stories. Our village is small — about 2,510 people — and that closeness is both a comfort and sometimes a pressure. Families lean on one another, but when money is short there aren’t many places to turn.

I finished junior high school (JSS/JHS) and then had to stop formal schooling. It wasn’t because I didn’t want to continue; it was because we simply could not afford the fees and supplies for senior high. My parents have always done what they can, but our household struggles. Right now there are six other people living in our house besides me: my mother, my father, my grandmother, two younger siblings and a cousin who lives with us. I sleep in a small room and share it with my youngest sister, who is eight years old — she’s the one child under 18 currently living in our home. Part of the reason I work part-time is to help provide for her and the others.

My part-time job is in the local market; I help my aunt sell Ghanaian staples and sometimes I make and sell akara or fried plantain in the afternoons. The income is small and irregular, but it helps cover basic things. On average our household spends about 60 cedis a week on food and only about 10 cedis on non-food items like water, electricity, and small contributions toward rent or school fees. With that budget, we have to be careful. If the market is slow or someone falls sick, everything gets stretched thin. That’s why I often describe our financial situation as bad — there’s a persistent worry about the next unexpected expense.

Health care is another challenge. The nearest clinic is a little over five kilometers away (about 5.09 km), which may not sound far if you have reliable transport, but for us it means a long walk or a costly motorbike ride. I remember the morning I had to take my sister the whole way because she had a fever; we had to leave early to avoid the midday heat and still ended up missing half a day of work. That distance factors into decisions about medical care and even about vaccines. If a new vaccine is offered nearby I would probably get it — I’d say there’s about a 62% chance I’d take the first shot in the first six weeks — but the cost and travel, plus uncertainty about side effects, make me pause.

Even though I live in a small community, my social network is wider than it may seem. I can readily name about 23 people who are close friends or relatives living nearby: neighbors, school friends, market people, and a few cousins. I also have family members in another village — six of them — and a handful of friends or acquaintances (about four) who live outside our immediate area. When I need to reach someone, I use my registered mobile phone number; having that line keeps me connected for emergencies and for checking on relatives in other villages. I don’t use social media at all — never have. My phone is for calls and the occasional SMS; I prefer talking in person or on the phone than scrolling through apps.

My days are a mix of routine and small emergencies. Mornings are for fetching water and preparing food for the household; then I head to the market to help set up the stall, barter for supplies, or take on odd jobs. Afternoons I might run errands, walk to the clinic if someone needs care, or help my younger siblings with whatever school tasks they have. There are quiet moments too — evenings when the family sits together and the radio plays softly, or when we share a plate and laugh about something that happened at the market.

I have hopes. I want to continue my education or learn a trade that can provide a steadier income — tailoring, for example, or formal small-business skills — so I can support my family better and give my little sister more opportunities. I also want better access to health services close to home; walking five kilometers for a check-up is exhausting and it keeps people from getting timely care.

Despite the hardships, I feel rooted here. People look out for each other, and I’ve learned to be resourceful. I am young, and I carry the weight of responsibility, but I also carry the stubborn optimism that comes from community ties and from knowing that small steady steps — a day’s earnings, a shared meal, an extra hour spent learning a new skill — can change the shape of what comes next.

I grew up in Asesewa Community D, a small place in the Upper Manya Krobo District of the Eastern Region where everyone knows everyone and the rhythm of life follows market days and harvests. I am 18 now, but I still remember the narrow dirt roads, the red dust that sticks to your feet in the dry season, and the evening hum of people sitting outside their compound walls telling stories. Our village is small — about 2,510 people — and that closeness is both a comfort and sometimes a pressure. Families lean on one another, but when money is short there aren’t many places to turn.

I finished junior high school (JSS/JHS) and then had to stop formal schooling. It wasn’t because I didn’t want to continue; it was because we simply could not afford the fees and supplies for senior high. My parents have always done what they can, but our household struggles. Right now there are six other people living in our house besides me: my mother, my father, my grandmother, two younger siblings and a cousin who lives with us. I sleep in a small room and share it with my youngest sister, who is eight years old — she’s the one child under 18 currently living in our home. Part of the reason I work part-time is to help provide for her and the others.

My part-time job is in the local market; I help my aunt sell Ghanaian staples and sometimes I make and sell akara or fried plantain in the afternoons. The income is small and irregular, but it helps cover basic things. On average our household spends about 60 cedis a week on food and only about 10 cedis on non-food items like water, electricity, and small contributions toward rent or school fees. With that budget, we have to be careful. If the market is slow or someone falls sick, everything gets stretched thin. That’s why I often describe our financial situation as bad — there’s a persistent worry about the next unexpected expense.

Health care is another challenge. The nearest clinic is a little over five kilometers away (about 5.09 km), which may not sound far if you have reliable transport, but for us it means a long walk or a costly motorbike ride. I remember the morning I had to take my sister the whole way because she had a fever; we had to leave early to avoid the midday heat and still ended up missing half a day of work. That distance factors into decisions about medical care and even about vaccines. If a new vaccine is offered nearby I would probably get it — I’d say there’s about a 62% chance I’d take the first shot in the first six weeks — but the cost and travel, plus uncertainty about side effects, make me pause.

Even though I live in a small community, my social network is wider than it may seem. I can readily name about 23 people who are close friends or relatives living nearby: neighbors, school friends, market people, and a few cousins. I also have family members in another village — six of them — and a handful of friends or acquaintances (about four) who live outside our immediate area. When I need to reach someone, I use my registered mobile phone number; having that line keeps me connected for emergencies and for checking on relatives in other villages. I don’t use social media at all — never have. My phone is for calls and the occasional SMS; I prefer talking in person or on the phone than scrolling through apps.

My days are a mix of routine and small emergencies. Mornings are for fetching water and preparing food for the household; then I head to the market to help set up the stall, barter for supplies, or take on odd jobs. Afternoons I might run errands, walk to the clinic if someone needs care, or help my younger siblings with whatever school tasks they have. There are quiet moments too — evenings when the family sits together and the radio plays softly, or when we share a plate and laugh about something that happened at the market.

I have hopes. I want to continue my education or learn a trade that can provide a steadier income — tailoring, for example, or formal small-business skills — so I can support my family better and give my little sister more opportunities. I also want better access to health services close to home; walking five kilometers for a check-up is exhausting and it keeps people from getting timely care.

Despite the hardships, I feel rooted here. People look out for each other, and I’ve learned to be resourceful. I am young, and I carry the weight of responsibility, but I also carry the stubborn optimism that comes from community ties and from knowing that small steady steps — a day’s earnings, a shared meal, an extra hour spent learning a new skill — can change the shape of what comes next.

I remember sitting at the table that morning on 13 February 2022, the rain having just stopped and a thin layer of dust still clinging to the veranda. I am 41 years old, a man who grew up in Kyeaboso, a small community in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region. Our village is tight-knit — about 1,498 people — and everyone knows your face and your story before you finish a sentence.

I left school after junior high, so my highest qualification is JSS/JHS. That basic schooling taught me to read, write a bit of English, and do arithmetic well enough to keep accounts and talk to traders. It was never easy deciding to stop at that level, but my family needed hands at home and I had to start working young. Those early responsibilities shaped me. I learned to be practical and to find solutions with what I had rather than waiting for someone else to provide them.

Today I work full time in Kyeaboso. I run a small business that supports the agricultural life here: I help organize the purchase and transport of cocoa and provide farming supplies to neighbors during planting season. The work keeps me awake before dawn and often busy until dusk — the rhythm of the land dictates my day. Some mornings I walk to meet farmers or to the roadside to wait for the lorry that will carry sacks to the buying center; other days I am at the shop, keeping ledgers on the same exercise book I’ve used for years. Having steady work is a relief — it allows me to provide for my household.

At home there are two people living with me right now, not counting myself. My wife and our youngest child. We get by together. On a typical week we spend about 50 Ghanaian cedis on food. That pays for staples — plantain, yams, gari, rice, some fish and the little things for our meals. We budget carefully; food is always the first priority. For non-food basics like electricity tokens, water, rent for the small room we keep, and school fees for our child, we spend roughly 100 cedis a week. Those expenses can feel heavy, but I would describe our household’s economic condition as good. We are not rich, but we are stable: bills get paid, there is food, the children can go to school, and we can handle small emergencies.

Living in Kyeaboso means I keep health close in my mind. The nearest health clinic is about 4.0 kilometers from where we live. It’s not exactly next door, so if someone is sick we have to plan for transport — a motorbike ride if we can afford it, or sometimes a long walk. That distance has made me cautious: I try to keep medicines at home for minor illnesses, and I support preventive measures when I can. I have a registered mobile number, which is important. I use it to coordinate with suppliers, call for transport, and keep in touch with family who live in nearby towns.

I’m practical but not careless about health decisions. For example, when vaccines became available, I remember thinking about the timing and weighing risks. If a COVID-19 vaccine had been available to me, I estimated there was about a 50% chance I would go for the first shot within six weeks of its availability. I wasn’t opposed, just cautious — wanting to see how others in the community reacted, to hear from the clinic staff, and to make sure that we could get there without causing problems at work or for the household. It was a balance between protecting my family and keeping our daily life running.

My community is where I draw strength. I know most of the farmers and traders by name. I help when I can — whether lending a sack of seed at planting time or offering a ride to the clinic. I am proud of the life we have built: a small business that keeps our heads above water, a family that eats together at the end of the day, and neighbors who look out for each other. I may not have gone further in formal education, but I have learned through labor, through the market, and through the small, steady responsibilities of being a husband, a father, and a working man in Kyeaboso.

I am 31 years old and I live in Sabina, a small community in the Assin North District of the Central Region. I grew up in this general area, the son of a family that moved often between a few nearby villages before finally settling here. I completed JSS/JHS and left school after junior high to help with the family work — there simply wasn’t the money to continue, and my time was needed on the farm and at the market. On 16 February 2022 I filled out an interview for a study about life in our community; that snapshot helped me think through what my days are really like.

I live in a busy house: there are seven other people besides me under our roof, and three children under 18. Between the children, my parents and a couple of younger siblings or extended relatives, the house never really sleeps. The whole village of Sabina is only about 834 people, but family ties stretch far — I can name twenty relatives who live in another village and another seven friends and acquaintances there. Close to home I really only have three people I can rely on every day for help or advice; people come and go, and a lot of family life happens over long distances.

Work occupies most of my time. I am employed full time — I run a small grocery and provisions shop in the market which I opened after years of selling produce from the farm. I also still do occasional farming during the season, planting cassava and maize with neighbors when we need labor exchange. Running the shop means early mornings and late evenings, balancing inventory and credit with customers, and trying to stretch the household budget. We spend about GHS 350 a week on food for everyone and around GHS 50 a week on non-food essentials like electricity, water contributions, and small school costs. That keeps us neither rich nor desperate — I would say our condition is neither good nor bad. We manage, but unexpected expenses can be a real worry.

Health and access to services shape much of how I plan my life. The nearest health clinic is not close — about 7.6 km away. For simple things I rely on a local drug vendor or an elder who knows traditional remedies, but for anything more serious it means a long walk or arranging transport, which is costly and time-consuming. That distance, along with mixed messages and worry about side effects, explains part of why I answered I was only 34% likely to get a first COVID-19 shot within the first six weeks if it were available to me — I’m cautious and I want to see how things play out before rushing.

I have a registered mobile number and I use it to keep in touch with distant family, to handle orders for the shop, and to call when I need help arranging transport. I never use social media — I prefer voice calls or meeting people in person, and my phone credit is better spent on calls than scrolling. My social life is practical: family responsibilities, work, children’s schooling, and the rhythms of farming and market days. I try to keep steady for the people in my house and for the twenty relatives who depend on me sometimes from other villages. That is how I live my life here in Sabina: rooted in family and work, cautious about risks, and always balancing the small daily needs against the hope that the larger things will get better.

I was born and raised in Kuntanase 3, a small but busy community in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District of the Central Region. Our village of about 2,006 people has a way of holding you close: everyone knows your name, and you know theirs. I finished my education at the SSS/SHS level and then stayed around here, building a life that mixes the old rhythms of village living with the steady demands of paid work.

I am 50 years old now. At home I live in a large compound with ten other people besides myself — a full house made up of grown children, siblings, an elderly parent, and a couple of younger relatives I help support. Only one child under 18 currently lives with us; the rest are adults who contribute in different ways. My household’s weekly food budget is about 300 Ghanaian cedis. That covers staples, some fresh produce and fish, and the occasional treat when there is cause to celebrate. Our non-food bills, though, are much larger: we spend roughly 7,000 cedis a week on things like rent for part of the compound, school fees for relatives who are in boarding, utilities, and payments we have agreed to shoulder for others in the extended family. Those figures surprise visitors, but when you account for the many shoulders I help carry — school fees, medical bills, rent top-ups for younger relatives trying to stand on their own — it all fits into the picture of how families here pool resources.

I work full time. My education stopped at SHS, but I’ve spent decades learning practically on the job. I’m employed in a managerial role at a local logistics and trading outfit that moves goods between towns and markets. The job keeps me busy — coordinating drivers, negotiating with traders, and ensuring deliveries reach their destinations on time. It’s honest work and it allows me to help the household financially, which is important to me. I don’t think of my life as poor or rich; if you asked me to rate our situation I’d say it’s neither good nor bad. We manage, sometimes we make sacrifices, sometimes we have small comforts. That balance is how I measure security now.

Health is never far from our minds. The nearest clinic is a bit more than five kilometres away — about 5.125 kilometres, in fact — which means a trip for minor issues and a longer trip when someone needs more serious care. I make sure people in my house attend to chronic conditions and that the child’s vaccinations and school health checks are kept up to date. I believe in modern medicine and I’m not a person who hesitates: when COVID vaccines became available, I decided immediately that I would take the first shot within the early weeks. I like to protect myself and those around me; that decision felt like the right, responsible thing to do.

My social circle is small and close. In the village I can count on three people — friends and relatives who live nearby — for day-to-day conversation, help with repairs, and the occasional drink under the mango tree. Beyond town I have one family member in another village and two friends or acquaintances in other places who I see when business or family needs bring us together. I’ve never taken to social media; I don’t use Facebook, WhatsApp groups, or Instagram. I have a registered mobile number and use it for calls and the occasional text. For me, relationships are built in person: a visit, a shared meal, a hand on the shoulder when someone faces trouble.

My days are practical. I wake early, meet drivers, check schedules, visit the market, handle paperwork, and then come home to the rhythms of a large household. Evenings are for listening — stories from people who grew up when the roads were dirt and the radios were new, updates from the young ones about their exams, and plans for how to manage next week’s fees or a needed repair. I take pride in being someone others can rely on without making a show of it.

Looking forward, my goals are simple: keep steady at work, keep the household fed and cared for, and see the younger ones through school so they can make choices I never had. I’m rooted in Kuntanase 3 and I feel the responsibility that comes with that root. The village shapes me as much as I try to shape the lives around me, and for now that is enough.

That balance is how I measure security now.

Health is never far from our minds. The nearest clinic is a bit more than five kilometres away — about 5.125 kilometres, in fact — which means a trip for minor issues and a longer trip when someone needs more serious care. I make sure people in my house attend to chronic conditions and that the child’s vaccinations and school health checks are kept up to date. I believe in modern medicine and I’m not a person who hesitates: when COVID vaccines became available, I decided immediately that I would take the first shot within the early weeks. I like to protect myself and those around me; that decision felt like the right, responsible thing to do.

My social circle is small and close. In the village I can count on three people — friends and relatives who live nearby — for day-to-day conversation, help with repairs, and the occasional drink under the mango tree. Beyond town I have one family member in another village and two friends or acquaintances in other places who I see when business or family needs bring us together. I’ve never taken to social media; I don’t use Facebook, WhatsApp groups, or Instagram. I have a registered mobile number and use it for calls and the occasional text. For me, relationships are built in person: a visit, a shared meal, a hand on the shoulder when someone faces trouble.

My days are practical. I wake early, meet drivers, check schedules, visit the market, handle paperwork, and then come home to the rhythms of a large household. Evenings are for listening — stories from people who grew up when the roads were dirt and the radios were new, updates from the young ones about their exams, and plans for how to manage next week’s fees or a needed repair. I take pride in being someone others can rely on without making a show of it.

Looking forward, my goals are simple: keep steady at work, keep the household fed and cared for, and see the younger ones through school so they can make choices I never had. I’m rooted in Kuntanase 3 and I feel the responsibility that comes with that root. The village shapes me as much as I try to shape the lives around me, and for now that is enough.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in MBRAA, a small but lively community in the Asikuma Odoben Brankwa District of the Central Region. The village is home to about 4,422 people, and I have known most of them in some way all my life. I finished Junior High School (JSS) and then started working to help my family — formal education ended early for me, but that pushed me to learn practical skills and to become independent quickly.

These days I’m 22 and employed full time. I work locally — my days start early, arranging produce and goods for the small stall I help run, then I head out to meet suppliers or serve customers from town. The job keeps me busy and gives me a steady income, which has made a big difference at home. There are three other people living in my house with me right now: my partner, my younger sister, and my mother. We also have one child under 18 in the house — my little one keeps us all on our toes and is the center of my world.

We spend about 210 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food. That covers the staples, fresh fish or chicken when we can, some vegetables, and little treats for the child. On non-food items — things like electricity, water, rent and school fees — we spend around 40 cedis weekly. For the size of our household and considering I didn’t have many formal qualifications, I feel fortunate; I’d describe our overall economic condition as very good. My steady work and careful budgeting have helped us feel secure, and we invest what we can into the child’s future.

Even though I work and get paid, I don’t have a registered mobile number set up to receive payments. We still handle most transactions in cash or through a family member’s mobile money when needed. It’s an inconvenient habit at times, but the community is close-knit and we manage.

One practical comfort is that the nearest health clinic is very close — only about 0.53 kilometers from where I live. That proximity matters to me. I remember the interview on 2022-02-08 when I was asked about vaccines. I thought about how important it is to stay healthy for my child and for my work, and I was willing — about an 83% chance I would get a first COVID-19 shot within six weeks of availability. I trust the clinic staff, and knowing I can walk there quickly makes it an easy choice. I want to be able to continue working, care for my family, and keep my child safe; those things guide most of my decisions.
