You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I am 45 years old, and I remember filling out that interview on 16 February 2022 at 03:47 in the morning—woke up early because my work day starts before sunrise. I grew up in the Central Region and still live in Assin North District, in a small community everyone calls Endwa Clinic. Our village is modest—about 1,454 people. It’s the kind of place where you know most faces, where children play in the dust after school and neighbors check on each other when rains come hard.

I finished Senior High School, and that education opened doors for me, even if it didn’t make life easy. Today I work full time at a small workshop in the district town. My job keeps food on the table and gives me a steady routine, but money is always tight. I live with four other people in the compound—my wife, two school-age children, and my elderly mother—so there are five of us altogether. We share one kitchen, one small sitting area, and whatever joy and worry come with living close.

On a typical week we spend about 100 Ghanaian cedis on food. Rice, gari, plantain, the occasional fish or goat meat when the budget allows—that’s what the money buys. For non-food basics—electricity, water, rent contributions, school supplies, small medicine needs—we manage with roughly 20 cedis a week. When I was asked to rate our household’s economic condition, I didn’t sugarcoat it: I said “bad.” There are months when the pay barely stretches to cover everything. I worry about school fees, about saving for rainy days, and about what will happen if one of us falls sick.

Healthcare access is one of those constant worries. Even though our community is called Endwa Clinic, the nearest proper health facility that can handle more serious issues is about 7.5 kilometers away. That distance matters. Getting there means a motorcycle taxi if someone can spare the fare, or a long walk if not. When my children have fevers or when my mother needs attention, that trip becomes an obstacle—time, money, and sometimes a day’s lost wage for me.

I’ve kept my life practical and connected; I have a registered mobile number and I use it to stay in touch with family, get news, and arrange work. During the pandemic, my phone became even more important—updates, announcements, and the occasional reminder about health measures. When asked how likely I was to take the first shot of a COVID-19 vaccine within six weeks of availability, I answered honestly: about 72 percent. I lean toward getting vaccinated because I want to protect my family and keep working, but I also have questions and watch how others respond before I act. There’s a mix of caution and responsibility in me.

My days are full—early mornings, the workshop, errands, and evenings spent helping the children with homework when I can. I take pride in providing for my family even if it’s a struggle. I try to teach my children the value of hard work and the importance of community. Sometimes at night I lie awake thinking of small improvements: better medical access, steadier income, and a little savings cushion so we don’t live month to month.

That is my life in Endwa Clinic—rooted in a small community, carrying responsibilities for those I love, balancing limited resources, and trying to make practical choices about health and future security.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I was born and raised in Kuntanase 2, and after sixty-nine years I still know every path and mango tree in the village. I learned to read and write only up to primary school, but life taught me the rest. For most of my working life I rose with the sun to tend small plots of cassava and cocoa, and some years I did seasonal work as a laborer and occasional market porter. Those hands and knees remember the work, and now that I am retired I prefer mornings on the porch, listening to the village wake up.

My house is small but full of life — two people live with me now besides myself: my wife, who still likes to plant vegetables in the little compound garden, and my granddaughter who comes here to study with me when the younger ones are away. We manage together. On average we spend about a hundred cedis a week on food; rice, gari, plantain, some fish when the market is good. Non-food things — kerosene, water, the small electricity bill — come to about fifteen cedis weekly. I’ll be honest, our finances are neither good nor bad; we have enough most weeks, and when we don’t there is always someone who will lend a hand.

Kuntanase 2 sits in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District in the Central Region, and our village is neither tiny nor large — about three and a half thousand people. The health clinic is not right next door; it’s a four-and-a-half kilometer walk, or a short motorbike ride when we need it quickly. I prefer to walk when weather and health allow. Over the years I have learned the faces at the clinic and the way nurses greet me, but I still keep a sharp eye on my joints and blood pressure.

I keep my world close. I have a mobile phone registered in my name; I use it for calls and to check in with family. I do not use social media — I never learned to and I do not miss it. My social network is real and physical: about ten people I can name who live nearby — old friends, cousins, the herbalist, the teacher who still complains about his students. I also have family spread out in other villages and towns; twelve members of my family live elsewhere, some who moved years ago for work or marriage. We write letters sometimes, but mostly we call.

The rhythms of life here are simple. I wake early, sit with a cup of hot water and reminisce, help with small chores, and in the afternoons I might mend a net, sharpen a machete, or share a story under the big ceiba tree with neighbors. At sixty-nine I find joy in small things: the taste of fresh cassava, the laugh of my granddaughter, the steady hum of village life. I answered the interview that cold morning of February 10, 2022 at dawn — perhaps that is why my memories were especially clear — and I hope this little account shows who I am: a retired man rooted in his land, living modestly, surrounded by family and neighbors, content with simple certainties.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I was born and raised in Kyeikrom, a small community tucked in the Assin North District of the Central Region. Our village is small — about six hundred ninety-five people — so everyone knows everyone’s story, and there is a rhythm to life here that I grew up with. I finished JSS and had hoped to continue, but school fees and the need to help at home meant I stopped after junior high. By nineteen I had become one of the main people my household counted on.

There are three other people living with me now: my mother, my younger sister, and my grandmother. My father left when I was small, and that absence has always made things tighter at home. We spend, on average, 210 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food — a surprisingly large slice of our expenses, but feeding four mouths takes most of what we earn. For non-food items — electricity, water, occasional fees — we only manage about fifteen cedis a week. It’s not enough for repairs, school books, or the things that might help us move forward. When I’m asked how our household is doing, I say “bad.” It’s the honest word: money is never steady, and small shocks — a sick child, a broken tool — can push us into real trouble.

I work full time. I wake up before dawn, walk past the baobab and the cassava heaps, and head to my job. Most days I’m on a nearby cocoa farm as a labourer during the harvest season and do odd jobs in the off-season — carrying sacks, doing paid weeding, sometimes loading produce onto a trotro bound for the district capital. I don’t own a tractor or big tools; my work is hands-on and physical. Employers pay me in cash, which is fine for paying for food, but annoying because I don’t have a registered mobile number where I can be paid digitally. I rely on other people’s phones or cash in hand. Not having a reliable mobile number limits me: no mobile money transfers straight to me, no easy contact with buyers in town, and sometimes I miss opportunities because someone can’t reach me.

Kyeikrom is small but proud. We have a single primary school, a small market on market days, and a community center where people meet to discuss issues. The nearest health clinic is about 4.6 kilometers away — not terribly far by some measures, but far enough when you’re sick, when the roads are muddy from the rains, or when you don’t have transport money. I remember carrying my grandmother on a makeshift stretcher when she had a fever; the walk to the clinic took hours and left us both exhausted. Those experiences sharpen your sense of vulnerability. Access to healthcare is patchy; sometimes the clinic runs out of medicine, and for anything serious you have to get a trotro to Assin to see a doctor.

Because of these realities, I think a lot about the future. I want to save, to send my sister further in school than I went, maybe start a small trading business in town. But savings are a dream for now. At the end of each week I set aside what I can, and sometimes that’s nothing. There’s pride in what I do — my hands know the land and the work — but there’s also worry that it won’t be enough to change things.

I was born and raised in Kyeikrom, a small community tucked in the Assin North District of the Central Region. Our village is small — about six hundred ninety-five people — so everyone knows everyone’s story, and there is a rhythm to life here that I grew up with. I finished JSS and had hoped to continue, but school fees and the need to help at home meant I stopped after junior high. By nineteen I had become one of the main people my household counted on.

There are three other people living with me now: my mother, my younger sister, and my grandmother. My father left when I was small, and that absence has always made things tighter at home. We spend, on average, 210 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food — a surprisingly large slice of our expenses, but feeding four mouths takes most of what we earn. For non-food items — electricity, water, occasional fees — we only manage about fifteen cedis a week. It’s not enough for repairs, school books, or the things that might help us move forward. When I’m asked how our household is doing, I say “bad.” It’s the honest word: money is never steady, and small shocks — a sick child, a broken tool — can push us into real trouble.

I work full time. I wake up before dawn, walk past the baobab and the cassava heaps, and head to my job. Most days I’m on a nearby cocoa farm as a labourer during the harvest season and do odd jobs in the off-season — carrying sacks, doing paid weeding, sometimes loading produce onto a trotro bound for the district capital. I don’t own a tractor or big tools; my work is hands-on and physical. Employers pay me in cash, which is fine for paying for food, but annoying because I don’t have a registered mobile number where I can be paid digitally. I rely on other people’s phones or cash in hand. Not having a reliable mobile number limits me: no mobile money transfers straight to me, no easy contact with buyers in town, and sometimes I miss opportunities because someone can’t reach me.

Kyeikrom is small but proud. We have a single primary school, a small market on market days, and a community center where people meet to discuss issues. The nearest health clinic is about 4.6 kilometers away — not terribly far by some measures, but far enough when you’re sick, when the roads are muddy from the rains, or when you don’t have transport money. I remember carrying my grandmother on a makeshift stretcher when she had a fever; the walk to the clinic took hours and left us both exhausted. Those experiences sharpen your sense of vulnerability. Access to healthcare is patchy; sometimes the clinic runs out of medicine, and for anything serious you have to get a trotro to Assin to see a doctor.

Because of these realities, I think a lot about the future. I want to save, to send my sister further in school than I went, maybe start a small trading business in town. But savings are a dream for now. At the end of each week I set aside what I can, and sometimes that’s nothing. There’s pride in what I do — my hands know the land and the work — but there’s also worry that it won’t be enough to change things.

When people ask if I’ll take the COVID-19 vaccine as soon as it becomes available, I say the chances are about sixty-five percent that I’ll go for the first shot within six weeks. That number comes from a mix of things: I want to protect my family and myself, and I’ve seen how sickness can ruin the little progress we make. But I’m cautious. I listen to neighbors, check what the clinic staff say when they come with information, and I want to be sure about side effects and how long I’ll need to rest afterward. Access is another worry — getting to the clinic on time, missing work, and losing a day’s pay. Still, if the health workers come to the community or if there’s a reliable outreach that explains things and makes it easy, I’ll be one of the first to go.

This is my life in Kyeikrom: hands stained with soil, early mornings, evenings filled with shared meals and hushed conversations about money and health. I carry responsibility and hope — weary sometimes, stubborn always — trying to make every cedi stretch toward a better tomorrow.

I filled out that interview on 21 February 2022, but my story begins long before that morning. I am thirty years old, born and raised in Akwamuman School Area, a tight-knit community tucked inside Asuogyaman District in the Eastern Region. Our village is small — only about 175 people — and everyone more or less knows everyone. That closeness shaped me: I learned early how much we depend on one another, from sharing farm tools to watching each other’s children when someone has to work.

I completed JSS/JHS and then stepped straight into work. Formal education stopped for me sooner than I had hoped, but it didn’t stop my determination. Today I am employed full time in the town nearby. My job is steady, with long days that often begin before the sun is up and end when I make the short walk home. Work gives me more than a wage; it gives me the routine and sense of purpose I value. I like knowing I can contribute reliably to our household.

At home I live with two other people — my partner and our little one, who is the only child under eighteen in our house. Our child keeps us busy and gives us a clear reason to plan ahead. We spend around 150 Ghanaian cedis a week on food: staples like fufu, rice, gari, fresh fish and vegetables, plus whatever little treats we can afford. Non-food costs — electricity, water, rent, occasional school fees or transport — come to about 50 cedis a week. Given those numbers, I rate our household’s economic condition as very good. We are not wealthy, but we have stability, and that stability feels priceless when you are trying to raise a family in a small community.

Our nearest health clinic is about 1.38 kilometers away — close enough that I can walk there in less than half an hour if needed, or just a five- to ten-minute motor-taxi ride. Having that access has been reassuring since I had my child, and it’s part of why I don’t worry overmuch about emergencies. I also keep a registered mobile number, which I use for everything from checking messages about work to staying in touch with family and getting updates from the clinic.

I am careful about health choices. When vaccines became available, I didn’t hesitate — I would take a first dose within the first six weeks if given the chance. My answer in the interview was 100% because I believe in protecting my child, my partner, and the neighbors I see every day. The decision was practical and personal: I want to keep my family healthy so we can keep working, learning, and sharing meals together.

Life here moves between the predictable and the small surprises. Weekends are for visiting relatives, borrowing a neighbor’s grinder for the yam, or taking the child down to the river to splash. I dream quietly of further training or courses that could open new opportunities, but for now I am content with what we have built: a warm home, a steady income, and a community that watches out for one another.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I filled out that interview on 21 February 2022, but my story begins long before that morning. I am thirty years old, born and raised in Akwamuman School Area, a tight-knit community tucked inside Asuogyaman District in the Eastern Region. Our village is small — only about 175 people — and everyone more or less knows everyone. That closeness shaped me: I learned early how much we depend on one another, from sharing farm tools to watching each other’s children when someone has to work.

I completed JSS/JHS and then stepped straight into work. Formal education stopped for me sooner than I had hoped, but it didn’t stop my determination. Today I am employed full time in the town nearby. My job is steady, with long days that often begin before the sun is up and end when I make the short walk home. Work gives me more than a wage; it gives me the routine and sense of purpose I value. I like knowing I can contribute reliably to our household.

At home I live with two other people — my partner and our little one, who is the only child under eighteen in our house. Our child keeps us busy and gives us a clear reason to plan ahead. We spend around 150 Ghanaian cedis a week on food: staples like fufu, rice, gari, fresh fish and vegetables, plus whatever little treats we can afford. Non-food costs — electricity, water, rent, occasional school fees or transport — come to about 50 cedis a week. Given those numbers, I rate our household’s economic condition as very good. We are not wealthy, but we have stability, and that stability feels priceless when you are trying to raise a family in a small community.

Our nearest health clinic is about 1.38 kilometers away — close enough that I can walk there in less than half an hour if needed, or just a five- to ten-minute motor-taxi ride. Having that access has been reassuring since I had my child, and it’s part of why I don’t worry overmuch about emergencies. I also keep a registered mobile number, which I use for everything from checking messages about work to staying in touch with family and getting updates from the clinic.

I am careful about health choices. When vaccines became available, I didn’t hesitate — I would take a first dose within the first six weeks if given the chance. My answer in the interview was 100% because I believe in protecting my child, my partner, and the neighbors I see every day. The decision was practical and personal: I want to keep my family healthy so we can keep working, learning, and sharing meals together.

Life here moves between the predictable and the small surprises. Weekends are for visiting relatives, borrowing a neighbor’s grinder for the yam, or taking the child down to the river to splash. I dream quietly of further training or courses that could open new opportunities, but for now I am content with what we have built: a warm home, a steady income, and a community that watches out for one another.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I woke up before dawn on 13 February 2022 and answered a long string of questions into my phone — the kind of morning when the village is still and the roosters haven't finished arguing. I live in Kotokye, a small community in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region. People here know one another by family name and by which mango tree you planted; our village has about 1,066 people, and most days the footpath to the market is busy with children and traders.

I am 31 years old. I completed Junior Secondary School (JSS/JHS), and that education shaped the way I look at the world even if I never finished senior high. I was young when life pulled me in other directions — family, children, responsibilities — and school was one of the first things to give way. I have three children under 18 living with me now. Together with them and my partner, we are four people sharing the house with me; our home is loud and alive, with cooking pots, schoolbooks, and the pulsing radio that keeps us informed.

I am not formally employed. Most days are spent tending the home, looking after the children, managing what we have, and helping with small agricultural chores when needed. My partner works — he is the main earner — and between his income, occasional sales of what we grow, and help from family, we manage. People would be surprised to hear me say our economic situation is “very good,” but compared with some neighbors we always have rice, gari, and palm oil on the table, and we can pay for the children’s school needs. On average we spend about 180 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food and another 140 cedis on non-food items like electricity, water, and school fees. Those numbers add up fast, but we make it work with careful planning and help when it’s needed.

The nearest health clinic is about 5.4 kilometers away. That distance matters — visiting the clinic means arranging someone to watch the children or taking a long walk or a costly motor-taxi. When a child has a fever or there is a vaccination drive, the trip becomes a full day. I have a mobile number registered in my name, which is useful for calls from relatives and for when the clinic or researchers need to reach me, but I do not use social media. I get news from the radio, from neighbors, and from conversations at the market or at church. Word-of-mouth shapes a lot of what I believe.

My wider family is spread out. There are about ten family members living in another village and some fifteen friends or acquaintances also in other villages. We visit each other when there is a funeral or a big celebration; otherwise we keep in touch by phone and occasional visits. That network matters: when money is tight someone will help, and when there is a question about a child’s health or where to go for supplies we call a cousin or a friend.

When it comes to new things — like a newly available vaccine — I am cautious. If a COVID-19 vaccine became available to me, I thought at the time I had only about a 20% chance of going for the first shot in the first six weeks. That number comes from many small reasons: worry about side effects, waiting to hear from people I trust who might have taken it, the trouble of taking three children to the clinic, and the distance to the health center. I would prefer to hear from the village nurse or from other women here who tried it and were fine; then I might go sooner. I am not closed off to modern medicine — I took my children to the clinic for routine shots as babies — but for something new I like to wait until I feel confident.

My life here is a mixture of steady routines and the little uncertainties that come with a rural household. I rise early, sweep the compound, cook, and make sure the children are ready for school. I sell small things sometimes — a bag of oranges after harvest or some eggs — and the income helps. We celebrate the harvest with neighbors, and we gather at the church on Sundays. I do not post my life online; instead, I learn and share aloud, face to face. That way I know who will come if I call them in the middle of the night, and who will bring cassava when we are short. That human closeness is my safety net, and it is how I have built a household that, despite the challenges, I consider very good.

My partner works — he is the main earner — and between his income, occasional sales of what we grow, and help from family, we manage. I answered the interview on the morning of 2022-02-05, and I remember sitting on the wooden bench outside my house as the sun was warming the red earth. I am fifty years old and I have lived most of my life here in Eshiem Odumasi, a small community in the Gomoa West District of the Central Region. My village is not large — about 1,736 people — and everyone knows each other. Being known has many comforts and some small obligations.

I never attended school. There was no chance for me to sit in a classroom when I was young; my days were needed at home and on the farm. I learned from my mother and neighbours how to plant cassava and maize, how to pound fufu, how to care for a child with a fever and how to stitch a torn dress. Those lessons have kept my family fed and clothed. I cannot read letters or fill forms easily, but I read faces and weather signs, and I know how to bargain at the market.

At home there are eight other people living with me right now, not counting myself. We are a busy household — four of those are children under eighteen. My days are full: before the sun gets high I prepare food, sweep the compound, send the older children to school and tend a small plot where I grow some vegetables and plantain. I am classed as unemployed because I do not have a steady paid job, but that does not mean I am idle. I cook, fetch water, look after the babies, help with farm work and sometimes I sell a few bundles of greens or roasted plantain at the market to add to the income.

Money comes into our household in small ways. Each week we spend about 170 Ghanaian Cedis on food — it’s the biggest part of our budget, and that goes fast when feeding nine people. Another 50 cedis goes toward non-food needs: a little for electricity when we can afford it, water, the small amount of rent we pay, and school fees or supplies for the children. By some luck and because we manage carefully, I would say our household is doing “good” right now — we are able to meet our needs, the children have clothes and are in school, and there is usually enough rice and gari in the store. That peace is precious to me.

I do not have a registered mobile number where payments can be sent to me. When money must be received or messages come, we use my husband’s or my eldest son’s phone, or someone in the neighbourhood will hold the phone for me. Mobile money could make things easier — I know that — but I have always relied on cash and the trust of my neighbours, so I have not set up my own account.

Health care is a worry because the nearest clinic is far — about 9.3 kilometres away. Going there is not a short walk, and it costs money for transport or a long day if you must walk. When a child has a fever or someone falls ill, we first try what we know at home: herbs, rest, and porridge. If it does not get better we will find a way to get them to the clinic, but the distance and cost make me cautious about going for every small thing.

I have thought about the COVID-19 vaccine. If you asked me on that morning in February, I would say there is only an 11% chance that I would choose to get a first shot within the first six weeks after it became available to me. I am not against medicine — I have taken injections before when it was necessary — but I worry. I worry about side effects and who will look after my family if I am sick for a few days after the vaccine. I have heard stories from people in the town, some true and some not, and without clear information and someone I trust nearby to explain, I prefer to wait and watch. The clinic being far makes it harder: I cannot easily go back and forth for follow-up or help if I need it.

My hopes are simple. I want the children to finish school so they do not have to live the same life I did without a classroom. I would like to start a little, steady business — maybe sell fish or open a small kiosk — but to do that I would need extra money and some help setting up a way to receive payments, maybe my own phone and a little training. I would like better access to health care in the community so we do not have to make that long journey when someone is sick.

This is my life: tied to the rhythms of the farm and the needs of my household, held together by the help of neighbours and family, cautious about new things and hopeful for the day when my grandchildren will have more choices than I did.

I remember the exact day I agreed to take part in the study — 5 February 2022 — because it felt like a small, important step of being counted and heard. I’m 25 years old, and I live in a tight-knit community called TARKWA ABOSO in the Gomoa West District of the Central region. Our village is small — about 1,201 people — so nearly everyone knows each other’s faces and stories. My household is always full: I live with eight other people besides myself, and among them are three children under 18. Some are my own children, some are younger cousins; we all share the same roof and the same small chores, worries, and laughter.

Education stopped for me after primary school. I didn’t go further because my family needed help at home and there wasn’t money for more schooling. Even so, the lessons I did get were important — they taught me to read a little, do sums, and to find ways to solve problems. Those early lessons became the foundation for how I manage our household now.

I work part time. Most days I split my time between helping with small trading activities and caring for the children and the home. I sell goods at the local market: sometimes fresh produce, sometimes gari and plantain, depending on what I can buy cheaply and what people want. The income is not steady, but with careful planning we stretch what we have. On average our household spends about 150 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. It may sound modest, but we plan meals that keep everyone fed. For non-food essentials — electricity, water, rent if any, and school-related costs — we manage with about 15 cedis a week. When I say our household condition is “good,” I mean that while we do not have much luxury, there is dignity and stability: food on the table, a roof, and people who look out for each other.

One of the practical difficulties of living here is access to health care. The nearest clinic is nearly 6.9 kilometres away. That distance matters when a child has a fever, when a mother needs antenatal care, or when we need medicine quickly. We usually walk part of the way and sometimes pay for a motorbike ride when we must. Having a registered mobile phone helps a lot — I can call relatives to arrange transport, get updates about market prices, or receive important news about the community. I have my own registered number and use it often to coordinate things.

Because I interact with many people at market and in the compound, I think a lot about health and safety. When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I didn’t hesitate — I would take the first shot within the first six weeks if it were offered to me. For me, getting vaccinated was about protecting my children, my neighbors, and my ability to work. It was about doing my part so the small household and the broader village can keep moving forward.

My days are full but steady: mornings begin early with cooking and sweeping, then off to the market to sell or to buy what we need, then afternoons of childcare, mending, or helping relatives with odd jobs. Nights are for family time — we share stories, talk about the next day’s plans, and hope for a little more stability and opportunity. I dream of learning a trade properly — tailoring or an improved trade business — so I can increase our income and maybe send the children to school for longer than I could.

I am proud of how we manage with what we have. Life here is a mix of challenge and warmth: the long walks to the clinic, the careful budgeting each week, the shared meals, and the certainty that when one of us needs help, someone else will be there.

I was born and raised in Kwabea Teryi, a small farming community in the Upper Manya Krobo District of the Eastern Region, and I have lived here my whole life. I learned by watching and doing: my mother taught me how to cook, how to tend the garden, and how to sew a stitch that will not come apart. Those hands-on skills became my education.

I work full time as a market trader and farmer. Each morning I wake before sunup to check on the plantain and cassava behind our compound, then I prepare things for the market — sorting, packing, bargaining. Trading keeps me busy and it keeps food on our table. My household spends about 210 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food and another 70 on non-food essentials like water, kerosene, electricity when we have it, and school supplies for the children. By the standards of my village, we are doing very well. We have a small savings habit, and I manage household money carefully; that’s why, when someone asks how our economic condition is, I say “very good.”

There are three people living with me besides myself: my husband and our two children, both under 18. The children go to the nearest junior high in the neighbouring town; we are proud that they are getting the schooling I never had. But it also means that information spreads fast, and sometimes rumours do too.

Health is one of the things I worry about because the nearest clinic is not close — it is about 10.3 kilometres away. A trip there means a whole day gone: walking or paying for transport, sitting and waiting, sometimes not even being able to see the nurse the first time. For minor ailments, we rely on home remedies first. For bigger matters, we make the journey. Having a registered mobile phone number helps a lot — I use my phone to call my sister in town, to hear market prices, and to get messages about important things in the district. I have heard many stories — some from people I trust, some from strangers — about side effects, about unknown long-term problems, and about how vaccines do not suit everyone. Because the clinic is far and because I am responsible for my family’s daily needs, I worry about taking something that might put me out of work for days. If you ask me right now, I would say the chance I would take a first shot within the first six weeks of availability is very small — only about five percent. That is not because I want harm to anyone; it’s because I have to balance risks with the very practical needs of my household.

My days are full but simple: tending the farm, going to market, cooking for the family, mending clothes late into the night when there is time. I keep a close eye on my children’s schooling and try to teach them what I can — how to bargain fairly at market, how to treat neighbours with respect, how to stretch a cedi so it lasts. Even without formal education, I have built a life that supports my family and my community. I am proud of that, and I continue to learn in the ways that matter to me and to the people I love.

I learned by watching and doing: my mother taught me how to cook, how to tend the garden, and how to sew a stitch that will not come apart. Those hands-on skills became my education.

I work full time as a market trader and farmer. Each morning I wake before sunup to check on the plantain and cassava behind our compound, then I prepare things for the market — sorting, packing, bargaining. Trading keeps me busy and it keeps food on our table. My household spends about 210 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food and another 70 on non-food essentials like water, kerosene, electricity when we have it, and school supplies for the children. I grew up in a small, close-knit place called Ekurakesse — one of those villages of about fifteen hundred souls where everybody knows your family’s story. I’m 26 now. As a boy I watched my uncles fix things around the compound, and that curiosity pushed me to enroll in a vocational school after junior high. I trained as an electrical/technical technician, learning to wire homes, repair small engines and keep pumps running. That hands-on training changed how I see work: I like solving problems with my hands and knowing my skill can put food on the table.

I started my current full-time job in early 2022, and since then my life has felt steadier. I live in a house with four other people — my wife, our young child, my mother and my younger sister — so there is always someone needing help, but also someone to share laughter with. We spend about 200 Ghana cedis a week on food; we eat well. Non-food items like electricity, water and school fees come to about 20 cedis a week. People might be surprised by those numbers, but for us they represent balance: we are comfortable and I would say our household’s financial condition is very good. I try to be responsible with my earnings; I send a little money to relatives in other villages when I can, because I have about thirty-five family members living elsewhere and I know how important that support can be.

My work keeps me busy most days. I usually leave the house early, ride a motorbike to nearby towns where I do installations and repairs, and come home in the late afternoon. When something major breaks down at the community borehole or a neighbor’s generator fails, people call me first. That responsibility feels good; being useful in a community of this size — with roughly sixteen hundred people — gives me a sense of purpose. I also maintain a broad local network: I can easily name a hundred people nearby who are friends or relatives and who I rely on for news, favors or work leads.

Health access is one of those everyday challenges. The nearest clinic is about 5.5 kilometres from our compound, so getting there means planning — either taking a motorbike taxi or arranging time off from work. My wife worries about the distance when the child is sick; I worry about missing work because our livelihood depends on regular jobs. I keep a registered mobile number, which helps a lot: I make appointments, call colleagues, and coordinate with relatives. Social media is part of how I stay connected too — I check Facebook and WhatsApp a few times a week to follow family updates, local job postings, and small-business groups that sometimes lead to work or parts I need.

I have friends and acquaintances spread out beyond Ekurakesse — about twenty-nine who live in other villages — and I try to keep those connections alive. Sometimes we exchange tools, sometimes advice, sometimes money. Family gatherings are loud and long; Sundays and market days are when we see most of the extended family and trade stories of work and plans. Even though I’m young, there’s an expectation that I’ll help the household and be present for relatives when they need me.

When it comes to healthcare choices like the COVID-19 vaccine, I’m cautious rather than opposed. If asked what the chances are that I’ll get the first shot within the first six weeks after it’s available to me, I’d say around thirty-one percent. I want to see how it affects people I know and whether it fits into our work schedule; I’m aware of the benefits, but new things make me pause until I have clear, practical reasons to act. I try to make decisions based on trusted advice from health workers or family members, and I ask questions first.

Looking ahead, I want to expand the small side business I’ve been building alongside my job — maybe a workshop where apprentices can learn the trade as I did. I’d also like to see better health access for people in our area; five and a half kilometres feels far when a child has a fever. For now I balance work, family and community, leaning on the skills I learned in vocational school and the network of people who make life in Ekurakesse both challenging and rewarding.

I try to be responsible with my earnings; I send a little money to relatives in other villages when I can, because I have about thirty-five family members living elsewhere and I know how important that support can be.

My work keeps me busy most days. I usually leave the house early, ride a motorbike to nearby towns where I do installations and repairs, and come home in the late afternoon. When something major breaks down at the community borehole or a neighbor’s generator fails, people call me first. That responsibility feels good; being useful in a community of this size — with roughly sixteen hundred people — gives me a sense of purpose. I also maintain a broad local network: I can easily name a hundred people nearby who are friends or relatives and who I rely on for news, favors or work leads.

Health access is one of those everyday challenges. The nearest clinic is about 5.5 kilometres from our compound, so getting there means planning — either taking a motorbike taxi or arranging time off from work. My wife worries about the distance when the child is sick; I worry about missing work because our livelihood depends on regular jobs. I keep a registered mobile number, which helps a lot: I make appointments, call colleagues, and coordinate with relatives. Social media is part of how I stay connected too — I check Facebook and WhatsApp a few times a week to follow family updates, local job postings, and small-business groups that sometimes lead to work or parts I need.

I have friends and acquaintances spread out beyond Ekurakesse — about twenty-nine who live in other villages — and I try to keep those connections alive. Sometimes we exchange tools, sometimes advice, sometimes money. Family gatherings are loud and long; Sundays and market days are when we see most of the extended family and trade stories of work and plans. Even though I’m young, there’s an expectation that I’ll help the household and be present for relatives when they need me.

When it comes to healthcare choices like the COVID-19 vaccine, I’m cautious rather than opposed. If asked what the chances are that I’ll get the first shot within the first six weeks after it’s available to me, I’d say around thirty-one percent. I want to see how it affects people I know and whether it fits into our work schedule; I’m aware of the benefits, but new things make me pause until I have clear, practical reasons to act. I try to make decisions based on trusted advice from health workers or family members, and I ask questions first.

Looking ahead, I want to expand the small side business I’ve been building alongside my job — maybe a workshop where apprentices can learn the trade as I did. I’d also like to see better health access for people in our area; five and a half kilometres feels far when a child has a fever. For now I balance work, family and community, leaning on the skills I learned in vocational school and the network of people who make life in Ekurakesse both challenging and rewarding.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I am twenty-six years old, born and raised in Korankyi, a small tight-knit community in the Asuogyaman District of the Eastern Region. Our village is tiny — only about 167 people — so everyone knows everyone. I never went to school. My parents couldn’t afford it when I was a child, and work was needed in the fields almost every day. I learned my trade the old way: watching, helping, listening to the elders, and picking things up with my hands. That is how I became who I am — practical, used to hard physical work, used to getting things done even when I can’t read and write.

I live in a small compound with my mother. It’s just the two of us at the moment — she depends on me for most things, and I depend on her for the quiet at home and the food she cooks. I am employed full time: I do manual labor and odd jobs around the district — sometimes I go to the farms to help with planting or harvesting, other times I do masonry, carry loads in the market, or take on any work a neighbor can pay me for. The work is steady some weeks and slow others; money is never as much as it should be.

We spend a lot on food — about 400 cedis each week. That covers staples like plantain, rice, cassava, fish when we can afford it, and vegetables. Most of our income goes straight to the market. Non-food items — water, a little electricity, small fees, and the occasional school-related expense for relatives — only come to about 30 cedis a week. After buying food and those few essentials, there is almost nothing left for savings or emergencies. That is why I say our household’s financial condition is bad. We live hand-to-mouth; if I miss work for a week, we feel it immediately.

The nearest health clinic is about 4.19 kilometers from my home. It might not sound very far, but when you have to walk, or when you don’t have money for transport, and when you’re carrying a heavy load from a day’s work, that distance is a real obstacle. Going to the clinic means losing a day’s wages for me, and sometimes it means borrowing transport money that we can’t spare. Because of that, we try to avoid going unless it’s necessary. My mother and I prefer home remedies first, then the clinic if nothing else works. The clinic staff are generally kind, but the journey and the cost make visits difficult.

I have a registered mobile number, and the phone is very important to me. Even though I never went to school, I learned how to use the phone early — for calls, for listening to radio programs, and sometimes to find out about work. People send messages and news over the network, and I listen. Still, a lot of information comes to me secondhand: through neighbors, through the market, and through what I hear at the church meeting or from the local chief. Trust is built locally. If the chief or a neighbor says something is good, I’ll pay attention; if it comes from a distant source, I want to see proof.

That is part of why I feel hesitant about new vaccines. When they talk about a COVID-19 vaccine, I think about the walk to the clinic, the worry about side effects that might keep me from working, and the mixed stories I hear on the radio and from friends. Right now, I would give myself maybe a ten percent chance of going to get the first shot within the first six weeks after it becomes available to me. I would rather watch and see how others in the community fare after taking it. If my mother needed it, or if my employer required it for work, I would take it then, but otherwise I would be cautious. There’s fear of being the first, and there’s the pressure of making sure I can work every day to keep food on our table.

My days are predictable: up before dawn, a quick meal, off to work until late afternoon, then back to cook and talk with my mother. Sundays are for church and for visiting neighbors. When I have a little money left, I dream small — maybe to save enough to start a small trading business, maybe to put my sister or a niece through school so they won’t have to make the same choices I did. I am proud of my ability to work and to take care of my mother, but I am also tired of worry. I want stability, a bit more money, and a future where health care and education are not choices we have to sacrifice. For now, I keep going, doing the work I know, holding onto what little we have, and watching the world change around me a step at a time.

I woke up that morning thinking about how the days keep passing, one small rhythm after another. I am 43 years old, a man who finished primary school and has learned most of what I need to know from life itself. I live in ABOMAYAW, a close-knit community in the Asuogyaman District of the Eastern Region. Our village is small — about fourteen hundred people — and everyone knows each other’s name, stories and struggles. I answered an interview on 21 February 2022 and it made me pause and remember the shape of my life.

At home we are eight in total: me and seven others who share the house with me. Four young faces in the house are children under eighteen — my children — and they are the reason I get up early each day. My wife helps with the home; there are also a couple of nieces and a younger brother staying with us from time to time when work is thin or school term breaks. Space is always full of voices and pots on the fire. We do our best to make the small compound comfortable and safe.

I work part time — the kind of work that comes and goes. Some weeks I have steady days lifting and carrying, helping people with small construction jobs, or selling produce when I can reach the larger market. Other weeks I patch together odd jobs: ferrying goods, fixing fences, anything that pays a little. Because of that irregularity, I have learned to plan carefully. On average we spend about 200 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. That covers the grain, vegetables, fish when it’s available, and the occasional treat for the children. Non-food expenses like electricity, water, rent and school contributions are tight; we manage with 20 cedis a week and a lot of careful juggling. I would describe our situation as neither good nor bad — we get by. Sometimes I worry about the next unexpected expense, but we manage.

School is important to me — not because I had much chance to study beyond primary level, but because I want more for my children. I try to encourage them, to help with homework when I can, and to save a little when the work is steady so they can stay in class. The cost of schooling and the small fees are always at the back of my mind when I think about sustainability.

Health is another thing that keeps me practical. The nearest health clinic is about 2.6 kilometers from our house — not too far, but far enough that a sick child or an elderly neighbor requires planning and sometimes a long walk. We have a registered mobile number, which helps when we need to call or arrange for transport or information. When the clinic is open and has medicine, we are grateful; when it’s closed or lacking supplies, we feel the worry more sharply.

About getting the COVID-19 vaccine: if the chance was measured in the first six weeks after it becomes available to me, I would put my likelihood at about 71 percent. I believe in protecting my family and myself. I have seen how illness can drain a household’s little savings, and I would rather prevent that. At the same time, I carry some concerns — new things make people in the village cautious, and I listen to stories and warnings. So I am keen but not perfectly certain; I would likely speak with the clinic staff and maybe a neighbor who has been vaccinated to be reassured before I go.

Life here is simple but full: we attend community meetings, I share news at the market when I go, and we help one another during harvest or when someone falls ill. My education may have stopped at primary level, but I have many lessons in patience, resourcefulness and caring for a family. My hopes are ordinary and strong: that my children grow up healthy and with more choices, that work steadies so we can save a little more, and that small, sensible decisions — like getting vaccinated when I feel ready — will keep us moving forward, together.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I was born and raised not far from here, in the Central Region, and my life has always been tied to the rhythms of our small community in Otukrom. I am 57 now, with a middle school education that stopped me from dreaming too far into the kinds of jobs the young people talk about, but it taught me enough to manage accounts at the market and keep my little household afloat. I began participating in a community study in February 2022, and answering those questions made me sit down and take stock of everything I carry with me every day.

My house is full—there are eight people living with me besides myself, and five of them are children under 18. They keep the house noisy and alive: the younger ones chasing one another through the courtyard, the older ones worrying about school fees and what they'll eat tomorrow. I work full-time; most days I am in the cocoa farms or doing odd jobs for neighbors, and sometimes I take on labor in the nearby town. The work is honest but hard. There are seasons when the yields are good, but too often the money comes in patchy and barely covers our costs.

We spend the equivalent of about 350 cedis a week on food. Good meals matter to me—seeing the children eat fills a part of the worry that this life gives me—but that amount doesn’t leave much for other things. Non-food expenses like electricity, water, rent, and school fees run us about 180 cedis a week. Between market trips, medicine, and school supplies, the money stretches thin and sometimes snaps. When I am asked to rate our household’s financial condition, I say “very bad” not because there is no hope, but because the day-to-day is a constant balancing act and I feel the weight of responsibility for every mouth at my table.

Health care is another constant concern. The nearest clinic is almost eight kilometers away. For a simple check-up it’s a long walk or an expensive trip by motorbike if the children are feverish and I can spare the money. I watch over them the best I can, but there are nights when I lie awake worrying about fever that might worsen before we get help.

I have a mobile phone and a registered number. It is essential—my lifeline to family and to work arrangements—but I don’t use social media. I prefer direct calls or sending a message when I must. My world is more tangible: neighbors, family, the market. Speaking of family, I have a large extended one—about fourteen family members live in another village. When there is a funeral or a wedding, every hand is needed; when there is a harvest, we help one another. Beyond those relatives, I can name around forty-two people I consider part of my social network—friends, traders, farmers, and neighbors who find a place in the daily exchange of news, goods, and favors.

Vaccination is something I think about with caution. I estimate about a fifty-one percent chance I would take a first COVID-19 shot within six weeks of it becoming available to me—half of me trusts the clinics and wants protection, and the other half worries about side effects, about taking time off work, and whether it will really help our situation. I balance fear and responsibility in everything—work, family, health.

My days begin before dawn. I boil water, prepare a simple breakfast, and send the children off to school if we can manage the fees. By midday I am at the farm or the market. In the evenings, we share stories, sometimes sing, sometimes argue about how to pay the next bill. I try to teach the children what little I know and encourage the older ones to learn more than I did. My hope is small but steady: that the kids will have a chance to study further, that we will not be sick at the wrong time, that the money will stretch just a little farther next month.

Life in Otukrom is not easy, but it is real. We hold on to each other, count our blessings quietly, and keep moving forward even when the road to the clinic or to a better harvest seems too long. I do what I can, with what I have, for those who depend on me.

I was born and raised in KAWANOAPDO, a small community tucked into the Central Region where the days move with the rhythm of farming seasons and market days. I finished only primary school; that was enough for the work I learned from my father and the older men in the village. I am 58 now, and most mornings I wake before sunrise to tend the cassava and maize plots behind our compound and then head into the township to my paid job. I am employed full time at a local milling cooperative — we grind and package staples for markets in neighboring towns. The work is steady and honest; it keeps a roof over our heads and food on the table.

Our house is busy. Besides me there are eight people living here right now, and four of them are children under eighteen — my youngest grandchildren and two nieces we took in when their mother fell ill. The compound is noisy and warm, filled with the smell of maize drying on mats and the chatter of children. We spend about one hundred cedis a week on food; that covers the yam, plantain, gari, fish and the little treats the children beg for. Another forty-five cedis goes toward non-food needs — kerosene, water contributions, the small school fees and the electricity bill when the power comes. I would say our situation is neither good nor bad; we make ends meet, but there is rarely much left over for anything extra.

Health care is always at the back of my mind. The nearest clinic is more than eight and a half kilometers away. When someone falls sick, the trip is a real journey — sometimes we must wait for a neighbor with a motorbike or save for transport. I worry about access for the older people in the compound, which is one reason I was quick to say I would get the COVID vaccine soon when it became available — I figure the chances I will take a first shot within the first weeks are high. I have a registered mobile number and use it mostly for calls; I never use social media. I keep my circle very small — I can really only name two people as close friends and relatives I rely on regularly: an older cousin who helps with the finances when needed, and a neighbor who watches the children when I have to work late.

My life is practical and full of small routines. I walk to the cooperative early, cut palm fronds for thatching when there is extra time, and on Fridays I go to the market to sell a little of our produce. I enjoy evenings sitting outside the compound, listening to the distant laughter and the calls of traders settling in for the night. I try to teach the children respect for hard work and the importance of looking after one another — the lessons I learned growing up here. There are worries, of course: money for school supplies, the long walk to the clinic, and the health of the older ones among us. But there is also comfort in the steady rhythm of work, the shared meals, and the small community bonds that keep us moving forward day by day.

I was born and raised in Beenuye, a small community in the Assin North District, and I still live here at sixty‑eight years old. This village of about four hundred seventeen people is where I learned everything I know — there were no school walls for me to sit behind, I never attended school, but I grew up watching and helping the older men and women in our family and community until I could do the work on my own. I cannot read or write in English, but I speak my local language well, I know numbers from years of trading and dividing cocoa and cassava, and I have a memory full of the practical lessons of a life outdoors.

I go to bed early and wake with the birds. My day begins before sunrise: I check the crops, mend a net or a tool if it needs fixing, and plan which fields I will tend that day. For most of my life I have been a farmer and a small trader — cocoa, plantain, cassava, a little vegetable garden and sometimes palm oil. Even now I work full time; at my age I can still walk the furrows, cut palm fronds, and carry sacks to the road for the trader’s pickup. Work keeps me active and gives me purpose. The money I earn from the farm and the small sales at market is steady enough that I describe our household’s condition as good.

At home there are four people living with me right now besides myself: my wife, our eldest daughter who helps with the house and the day market, and two grandchildren who run and laugh and keep us young. We are a close household and we share everything. On a typical week we spend about one hundred cedis on food — that covers the staples, some fish or meat now and then, oil, salt, and what the children need. We also spend about thirty cedis a week on non‑food items: kerosene or a little petrol, water when the rains are low, some school supplies for the grandchildren, and occasional fees. For a village life, this keeps us comfortable; we may not have many luxuries, but there is enough.

There are challenges, too. The nearest health clinic is eight and a half kilometres away. That distance is not easy when someone is sick and there is no quick transport. I remember walking that road many times, or paying for a motorbike if we must. When the rains are heavy the path becomes slippery and slow. Because I do not have a registered mobile number — I never got one for myself — I rely on neighbors and my children to call ahead if we need to arrange a pick‑up or to speak with someone in town. People ask me why I do not have a phone; the truth is, I prefer to keep my life simple and I trust the small network here in the village. When I need money moved, I walk to the trading center, or my daughter will go and take care of payments and messages.

I felt the weight of the COVID time like everyone. I remember the worry as news came slowly to our village, the discussions under the big ceiba tree, and the visits to the clinic to learn what precautions we should take. When asked about a first vaccine shot if it became available, I thought about my grandchildren and my wife and how I would not want to bring sickness home to them. I am not one for quick decisions, but I believe in the doctors and the nurses at the clinic, and I have seen what vaccines have done for other diseases over the years. I would be likely — about eighty percent sure — to take the first shot within six weeks of it being available to me. I want to protect my family, and I trust that getting vaccinated is part of keeping our small household safe so we can keep working and living our days.

I know the rhythm of our community: births, funerals, market days, and naming ceremonies. I take part in the local sharing of labor during harvests, and neighbors help each other when a roof needs mending or a sick child needs company. My life has been built on those ties. I may not have a certificate on a wall, but I have hands worn by honest work, a store of stories and skills, and the respect of my neighbors. When I was interviewed on the early morning of 2022‑02‑18, I answered truthfully about my life — the small comforts, the long walks to the clinic, the work that keeps me going — and I remain grateful for what we have in Beenuye.

I wake before dawn most days, and that morning of February 14, 2022 at 7:00 a.m. was no different. I live in Mirekukrom, a small community of about 629 people in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region, and mornings here feel like the whole village is rising at once — roosters, motorbikes, neighbors calling across compounds. I am 29 years old, a woman who finished junior high school (JSS/JHS), and I work full time to keep our household afloat.

My family and I live in a simple compound house where six other people share the space with me: my father, my mother, my younger brother, my sister-in-law, my husband’s uncle, and my own child — the little one who keeps me on my toes and is the only child under 18 living with us. Life is busy and crowded, but it also feels safe because we look out for one another. Because my education stopped after JHS, I could not take the long route to higher school; instead I learned hands-on skills from my mother and neighbors, and I started working early to help with household expenses.

I am employed full time at a small agro-processing center in the nearest town. My day begins around 5:30 a.m.: I fetch water, help get my child ready for the makeshift daycare run by my sister-in-law, and walk or catch a shared motorbike to work. The commute is part of the grind — many essential services are far from Mirekukrom. The nearest health clinic is nearly 8.8 kilometers away, which matters whenever someone in the family falls ill or when my child needs routine checks. It is a long trip on a bad road, and it reminds me how thin the safety net is for people in our village.

At work I handle packing and weighing crops, answering customers when traders come in, and keeping simple accounts on paper. The job pays modestly, but because it is steady, it has become the backbone of our household income. I spend about 55 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food for the family — that has to stretch across shared meals, school snacks, and the occasional protein when money allows. Despite working full time, I would describe our economic condition as bad; unexpected expenses like a child’s medicine or repairs can push us into uncertainty. We try to economize — growing some vegetables near the compound, buying in bulk when possible, and pooling resources with relatives.

There are days when I feel tired and frustrated. The village feels small sometimes, and opportunities for someone with my level of education are limited. But there is also a stubborn hope in me. I am determined that my child will have more choices: better schooling, maybe a trade or further education, and the freedom to pursue work without the constraints I faced. That hope is why I answer the phone when I get calls with information about training opportunities or community programs. I do have a registered mobile number, and that connection to the wider world is valuable.

Health is always on my mind because of the long distance to the clinic. When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I was ready to take them — I believed in protecting my child, my family, and my neighbors. I estimated a 91% chance I would get the first shot within six weeks of availability; for me it wasn’t just about me, it was about being able to keep working and caring for others without fear. Access can be a barrier, but when there is a chance to protect ourselves, I want to take it.

Evenings are for family. After I return from work, we share food, talk about the day, and plan what we can do for tomorrow. I dream of saving enough to fix the roof properly, to send my child to better school, and maybe one day to take a short course that will open new doors. For now, I keep going — balancing full-time work, childcare, and the responsibilities that come with being part of a large household in a small village. I wake before dawn most days, and that morning of February 14, 2022 at 7:00 a.m. was no different. I live in Mirekukrom, a small community of about 629 people in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region, and mornings here feel like the whole village is rising at once — roosters, motorbikes, neighbors calling across compounds. I am 29 years old, a woman who finished junior high school (JSS/JHS), and I work full time to keep our household afloat.

My family and I live in a simple compound house where six other people share the space with me: my father, my mother, my younger brother, my sister-in-law, my husband’s uncle, and my own child — the little one who keeps me on my toes and is the only child under 18 living with us. Life is busy and crowded, but it also feels safe because we look out for one another. Because my education stopped after JHS, I could not take the long route to higher school; instead I learned hands-on skills from my mother and neighbors, and I started working early to help with household expenses.

I am employed full time at a small agro-processing center in the nearest town. My day begins around 5:30 a.m.: I fetch water, help get my child ready for the makeshift daycare run by my sister-in-law, and walk or catch a shared motorbike to work. The commute is part of the grind — many essential services are far from Mirekukrom. The nearest health clinic is nearly 8.8 kilometers away, which matters whenever someone in the family falls ill or when my child needs routine checks. It is a long trip on a bad road, and it reminds me how thin the safety net is for people in our village.

At work I handle packing and weighing crops, answering customers when traders come in, and keeping simple accounts on paper. The job pays modestly, but because it is steady, it has become the backbone of our household income. I spend about 55 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food for the family — that has to stretch across shared meals, school snacks, and the occasional protein when money allows. Despite working full time, I would describe our economic condition as bad; unexpected expenses like a child’s medicine or repairs can push us into uncertainty. We try to economize — growing some vegetables near the compound, buying in bulk when possible, and pooling resources with relatives.

There are days when I feel tired and frustrated. The village feels small sometimes, and opportunities for someone with my level of education are limited. But there is also a stubborn hope in me. I am determined that my child will have more choices: better schooling, maybe a trade or further education, and the freedom to pursue work without the constraints I faced. That hope is why I answer the phone when I get calls with information about training opportunities or community programs. I do have a registered mobile number, and that connection to the wider world is valuable.

Health is always on my mind because of the long distance to the clinic. When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I was ready to take them — I believed in protecting my child, my family, and my neighbors. I estimated a 91% chance I would get the first shot within six weeks of availability; for me it wasn’t just about me, it was about being able to keep working and caring for others without fear. Access can be a barrier, but when there is a chance to protect ourselves, I want to take it.

Evenings are for family. After I return from work, we share food, talk about the day, and plan what we can do for tomorrow. I dream of saving enough to fix the roof properly, to send my child to better school, and maybe one day to take a short course that will open new doors. For now, I keep going — balancing full-time work, childcare, and the responsibilities that come with being part of a large household in a small village. Life here is hard, but it is also full of small kindnesses, and those keep me moving forward.

I grew up in Kuntanase 2, a small, dusty stretch of homes and cocoa farms in the heart of the Central Region. I am twenty now, but in many ways I still feel like the little girl who ran barefoot to fetch water at sunrise and raced the other children to the mango tree. Our village only has about three and a half thousand people, so faces become familiar quickly—my neighbor’s laugh, the market woman’s call, the sound of the motorbike that brings goods from town once or twice a week.

My education stopped after primary school. At the time, my family needed hands more than homework: there were chores to do, little money to stretch, and later the baby that changed everything. I live in a small compound with four other people—my mother, my younger sister, my grandfather, and my little boy. Having a child so young taught me responsibility in a way school never could. I am unemployed at the moment; I try to pick up odd jobs when I can—sweeping the church, helping in the cassava drying field, carrying bundles to the roadside for traders—anything that brings a bit of cash. Mostly I look after the house, cook, and take care of my son while my mother helps whenever she can.

Money is always a daily calculation. Our household spends around 350 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. That covers fufu and soup, gari, plantain, rice, oil, and the occasional goat meat when there is extra. Food is non-negotiable; we eat first. But for everything else—light, water, small school things for my sister, transport—that comes to maybe fifteen cedis a week. It’s tight, and sometimes we have to borrow or leave items unpaid. I don’t think we are poor in the absolute sense—my mother manages to keep the roof over our heads and meals on the table—but we are not comfortable. I would say our financial condition is neither good nor bad. It is a steady tightrope.

Health is a worry because the nearest clinic is almost five kilometers away—about a 4.66 km walk if there is no motorbike. With a little one on my back or on my hip, that distance feels long. When my son had fever last year, the walk and the waiting at the clinic made me anxious. For minor illnesses, we rely on the community health volunteer or the herbal remedies elders know, but for anything more serious the distance becomes a real barrier. Still, I have a mobile number registered; my phone is not new or fancy, but it is mine, and I use it to get information. I’ve received messages about health outreaches and vaccine days, and I’m careful to listen.

When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I did not hesitate. If someone asked me in those first six weeks whether I would take the first shot, I would have said yes without thinking twice. My decision was simple: I have a child and a family who depend on me. I want to be around for him. The thought of getting sick and not having the strength to care for him terrifies me more than any fear about a vaccine. Besides, the nurses who came to town explained the vaccines, and my mother convinced me as well. Having that information and support matters.

My days begin early. I wake before sunrise, sweep the compound, fetch water if the tap is slow, and prepare breakfast. I bathe my son, dress him, and if I have work I’ll head out to the farms or the market. If there’s no work, I sit and mend, chat with neighbors, or try to save enough to start a small trade—soaps and sachet water, maybe, so I can build something steady. In the evenings, we share the day’s stories, cook together, and sometimes listen to the radio when the batteries allow. I dream of going back to school someday, of taking a short vocational course to learn tailoring or hairdressing so I can have a regular income. For now, my goals are small and concrete: keep my son fed, try to save a little each week, and make sure we stay healthy.

Life here can be hard, but it is full of community. When someone’s child is sick, neighbors bring porridge; when a farm yields cocoa, we celebrate together. I know the road ahead will require patience, hard work, and perhaps some help from programs that bring services closer to villages like mine. Until then, I do what I can—care for my family, keep hope alive, and say yes to what keeps us safe, like the vaccine that I was ready to take as soon as it was offered.

I grew up in Kuntanase 2, a small, dusty stretch of homes and cocoa farms in the heart of the Central Region. I am twenty now, but in many ways I still feel like the little girl who ran barefoot to fetch water at sunrise and raced the other children to the mango tree. Our village only has about three and a half thousand people, so faces become familiar quickly—my neighbor’s laugh, the market woman’s call, the sound of the motorbike that brings goods from town once or twice a week.

My education stopped after primary school. At the time, my family needed hands more than homework: there were chores to do, little money to stretch, and later the baby that changed everything. I live in a small compound with four other people—my mother, my younger sister, my grandfather, and my little boy. Having a child so young taught me responsibility in a way school never could. I am unemployed at the moment; I try to pick up odd jobs when I can—sweeping the church, helping in the cassava drying field, carrying bundles to the roadside for traders—anything that brings a bit of cash. Mostly I look after the house, cook, and take care of my son while my mother helps whenever she can.

Money is always a daily calculation. Our household spends around 350 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. That covers fufu and soup, gari, plantain, rice, oil, and the occasional goat meat when there is extra. Food is non-negotiable; we eat first. But for everything else—light, water, small school things for my sister, transport—that comes to maybe fifteen cedis a week. It’s tight, and sometimes we have to borrow or leave items unpaid. I don’t think we are poor in the absolute sense—my mother manages to keep the roof over our heads and meals on the table—but we are not comfortable. I would say our financial condition is neither good nor bad. It is a steady tightrope.

Health is a worry because the nearest clinic is almost five kilometers away—about a 4.66 km walk if there is no motorbike. With a little one on my back or on my hip, that distance feels long. When my son had fever last year, the walk and the waiting at the clinic made me anxious. For minor illnesses, we rely on the community health volunteer or the herbal remedies elders know, but for anything more serious the distance becomes a real barrier. Still, I have a mobile number registered; my phone is not new or fancy, but it is mine, and I use it to get information. I’ve received messages about health outreaches and vaccine days, and I’m careful to listen.

When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I did not hesitate. If someone asked me in those first six weeks whether I would take the first shot, I would have said yes without thinking twice. My decision was simple: I have a child and a family who depend on me. I want to be around for him. The thought of getting sick and not having the strength to care for him terrifies me more than any fear about a vaccine. Besides, the nurses who came to town explained the vaccines, and my mother convinced me as well. Having that information and support matters.

My days begin early. I wake before sunrise, sweep the compound, fetch water if the tap is slow, and prepare breakfast. I bathe my son, dress him, and if I have work I’ll head out to the farms or the market. If there’s no work, I sit and mend, chat with neighbors, or try to save enough to start a small trade—soaps and sachet water, maybe, so I can build something steady. In the evenings, we share the day’s stories, cook together, and sometimes listen to the radio when the batteries allow. I dream of going back to school someday, of taking a short vocational course to learn tailoring or hairdressing so I can have a regular income. For now, my goals are small and concrete: keep my son fed, try to save a little each week, and make sure we stay healthy.

Life here can be hard, but it is full of community. When someone’s child is sick, neighbors bring porridge; when a farm yields cocoa, we celebrate together. I know the road ahead will require patience, hard work, and perhaps some help from programs that bring services closer to villages like mine. Until then, I do what I can—care for my family, keep hope alive, and say yes to what keeps us safe, like the vaccine that I was ready to take as soon as it was offered.
