I was born and raised in Abease, a small, dusty village in the Assin North District of the Central Region. Our village is the kind of place where everybody knows each other — there are about 855 people here — and life moves with the rhythm of the market days, the cocoa season, and the rains. I finished primary school, and that is the highest level of schooling I have completed. I remember the classrooms, the chalk dust, and the feeling that I needed to help my family more than I needed another year at school.

I am nineteen now and work full time. I learned how to sew from my aunt when I was young, and over the last few years I have built it into a steady way to support myself and my family. My days start early: by dawn I am at the sewing machine — hemming, fixing, making simple dresses and alterations for neighbors and people who come from the nearby towns. When the market is on, I help my mother sell some of the things we grow and the small items we buy to resell. People usually pay me in cash; I don’t have a registered mobile number for payments, so mobile money transfers are rarely an option for me. Because of that, I keep my earnings in a small box at home or I hand them over to my mother until we need them.

I live in a crowded but warm house with nine other people — not counting me — so there’s always laughter, arguing, and the smell of food. My household is made up of my parents, two younger siblings, my grandmother, an uncle and his two children, and a cousin who helps with cooking. We share everything: chores, meals, and the small profits from selling fresh tomatoes, gari, and the garments I sew. Even though we are many under one roof, we manage our money carefully. On an average week we spend about 240 Ghanaian cedis on food and another 100 cedis on non-food items like electricity, water and the small school fees for the younger children. For people in our village that level of regular spending feels comfortable, and I would say our household’s economic condition is good — not rich, but steady and secure enough that we do not worry every day about where the next meal will come from.

Living here means learning to be resourceful. The nearest health clinic is about 6.36 kilometers away, so we do not go there for every small problem. A trip to the clinic is a day-long affair: we save money for transport, sometimes walk part of the way, and only go when someone is really sick or for scheduled services. That distance made me think carefully when COVID vaccines became available. I answered a survey saying I would take the first shot within six weeks if it were available to me — and I mean it. I have seen sickness take people away, and protecting myself and my family feels like another job I must do well. If the clinic can arrange a vaccination outreach closer to the village, I will be there first in line.

I still have dreams beyond what I do now. I would like to save enough to buy a better sewing machine, maybe open a small shop in the market so I can hire a young person from the village to help. I would love to go back to school someday, even if it is night classes or short courses in tailoring and business. For now, I take pride in the life we have built: the noise of the compound at dinner time, the clients who bring me fabric with trust, and the steady way our household money keeps the lights on and food on the table. I am young, tied to my family, and doing the work that keeps us going — and I carry hope for something more.

I was born and raised in Abodwese, a small farming community in the Assin North District of the Central Region, where nearly a thousand people know each other by name. I am 22 years old, and my childhood here shaped who I am—close to family, used to long walks, and respectful of traditions. I finished junior high school and that’s as far as my formal education went. School was important to my parents, but life had other plans: after JHS I took on work to help support my mother, my younger siblings and our extended household.

We live in a compound house that has eight people in it counting me. Besides me there are seven others—my mother, an older aunt, two younger brothers, and three children under 18 who depend on us; they are my younger cousins and siblings whom I help raise. There’s always noise and laughter in the mornings as the children get ready for school and someone prepares breakfast. Food is central to our days: we spend about 300 Ghanaian cedis a week on food. With so many mouths to feed, it adds up quickly—maize, rice, gari, garden eggs, plantains, and the occasional fish or goat meat when we can afford it. Non-food expenses are surprisingly small—only about 10 cedis a week—because we don’t pay rent and our water and electricity are irregular or shared, so most weeks there’s not much to spend on utilities beyond a little kerosene or phone credit.

I work full time in the local market as a trader and seamstress’s assistant. In the mornings I wake before dawn to help my mother prepare food and see the children off. By seven I’m at the market, selling cassava or helping a seamstress sew clothes for people from surrounding towns. It’s honest work and steady enough to cover food and small school fees when needed. Some weeks are better than others—during harvest or market days I make more, and sometimes I tuck small savings away for emergencies. Overall, I would describe our household’s financial situation as neither good nor bad: we manage, but any sudden illness or expense could unsettle things.

Health and access to services are constant considerations. The nearest health clinic is about 6.36 kilometers away. That distance matters when someone is sick; we don’t always have money for transport and often walk or hire a motorbike if it’s urgent. For the three children in the house, I worry about delays in getting care. Still, we rely on the local nurses when they come for outreach and on traditional remedies when we must.

I have a registered mobile number and use it every day—calls to check on relatives, to arrange sales, to receive short messages about market days or health information. Mobile money has become useful for sending small amounts to relatives in town and for receiving payments. When a health team visited last year to talk about COVID-19 vaccines, I listened closely. I trust the nurses who come from the clinic and I want to protect my family—especially the children—from sickness. If a vaccine is available to me, there’s a very high chance I will take it within the first six weeks because I think it’s important for the people I care for and for keeping my ability to work.

Looking ahead, I want to learn more skills so I can improve our situation. I save a little from each week to buy better sewing equipment or to start a small bakery or food stand near the market. I dream of a future where my younger siblings finish school and where we have a small, steady income that keeps the children healthy and gives us a bit more security. For now, I keep pushing—balancing markets, family, and the everyday tasks of life in Abodwese—holding onto hope and practical plans for a better tomorrow.

I remember the morning they asked me these questions — it was 14 February 2022, and I woke before sunrise, as I usually do. I live in Kwadia, a small place in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region. Our village is tiny — only about 296 people — so everyone knows one another. I am 30 years old and I have never attended school. I learned most things by watching, listening and doing: how to peel cassava, how to tell when a yam is ready for market, how to calm a crying child. Reading and writing are things I long for sometimes, but life has kept me busy with work and family.

My home is crowded in the way many Ghanaian houses are — not because we want it that way, but because we need the help and company. There are five other people living with me right now, not counting myself. One child under 18 is in the house; she is my daughter and the center of much of my planning and worry. The rest are a mixture of older relatives and sometimes a niece or uncle who stays with us when times are hard elsewhere. We survive together, sharing food, chores and whatever money comes in.

Work is part-time for me. I do a bit of everything—some days I go to the farm to help with cassava or plantain, other days I carry produce to the nearby town market, sometimes I help a neighbor with weaving or petty trading. The income is never steady and never enough. On an average week we spend about 35 Ghanaian cedis on food for the whole household. That amount has to stretch across porridge, gari, yams, a little oil and sometimes fish. When the money runs short, we skip treats, we eat more yam and less fish, and we accept invitations to help on other farms in exchange for a little food or cash. Because of all this I would describe our household’s economic condition as bad. There are nights I lie awake wondering how we will pay for school uniforms or a sick visit if it comes.

Health care is a worry because the nearest clinic is not close — it’s over 10 kilometers away. That distance matters. If someone is feverish in the night we wait and pray, because hiring a motorbike taxi costs more than it feels like we can spare and walking takes too long and is hard with a sick child. I remember carrying my niece on my back to a clinic years ago, the sun burning and the path hot and rocky. Those trips take a whole morning and sometimes the medicines we need are not in stock. For serious problems, people in the village sometimes prefer to save and go to the hospital in the town, but that is expensive. I would go for vaccination when it becomes available — I said there is a 76 percent chance I would take the first shot within six weeks — I trust the health workers and want to protect my family, but I also worry about side effects and the cost of travel to get the shot.

Even without formal schooling, I value knowledge. I have a registered mobile phone and it is a lifeline: I get market prices, calls from relatives in town, and messages about clinic days or where there is work. But the phone also brings its own strain — buying airtime or charging the battery when power is unreliable adds to the list of small costs that add up. I remember the little joy of a text from my cousin when she got a job; those moments remind me that life can change.

My days are full of small rhythms: cooking starch in the early hours, tending a small plot, walking to the market some mornings, watching my daughter practice the things I can teach her, and saving tiny coins when I can. I worry about the future — I want my daughter to go to school and learn to read, to have choices I never had. I want a more secure roof over our heads and a way to get to the clinic without counting and recounting cedis.

Community ties keep me going. When someone is in trouble we share food and labor. When the harvest is good, neighbors come together to celebrate. When it isn’t, we sit and plan. I try to be hopeful. Every time I see a health worker at a community meeting or hear of a job in town, I think of small steps forward. I may not have had a classroom, but I have learned resilience, care and how to stretch what little we have. Those are the lessons I pass on to my daughter as we walk the dusty path of Kwadia together.

I live in Kwadia, a small place in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District of the Central Region. Our village is tiny — only about 296 people — so everyone knows one another. I am 30 years old and I have never attended school. I learned most things by watching, listening and doing: how to peel cassava, how to tell when a yam is ready for market, how to calm a crying child. Reading and writing are things I long for sometimes, but life has kept me busy with work and family.

My home is crowded in the way many Ghanaian houses are — not because we want it that way, but because we need the help and company. There are five other people living with me right now, not counting myself. One child under 18 is in the house; she is my daughter and the center of much of my planning and worry. The rest are a mixture of older relatives and sometimes a niece or uncle who stays with us when times are hard elsewhere. We survive together, sharing food, chores and whatever money comes in.

Work is part-time for me. I do a bit of everything—some days I go to the farm to help with cassava or plantain, other days I carry produce to the nearby town market, sometimes I help a neighbor with weaving or petty trading. The income is never steady and never enough. On an average week we spend about 35 Ghanaian cedis on food for the whole household. That amount has to stretch across porridge, gari, yams, a little oil and sometimes fish. When the money runs short, we skip treats, we eat more yam and less fish, and we accept invitations to help on other farms in exchange for a little food or cash. Because of all this I would describe our household’s economic condition as bad. There are nights I lie awake wondering how we will pay for school uniforms or a sick visit if it comes.

I remember carrying my niece on my back to a clinic years ago, the sun burning and the path hot and rocky. Those trips take a whole morning and sometimes the medicines we need are not in stock. For serious problems, people in the village sometimes prefer to save and go to the hospital in the town, but that is expensive. I would go for vaccination when it becomes available — I said there is a 76 percent chance I would take the first shot within six weeks — I trust the health workers and want to protect my family, but I also worry about side effects and the cost of travel to get the shot.

Even without formal schooling, I value knowledge. I have a registered mobile phone and it is a lifeline: I get market prices, calls from relatives in town, and messages about clinic days or where there is work. But the phone also brings its own strain — buying airtime or charging the battery when power is unreliable adds to the list of small costs that add up. I remember the little joy of a text from my cousin when she got a job; those moments remind me that life can change.

My days are full of small rhythms: cooking starch in the early hours, tending a small plot, walking to the market some mornings, watching my daughter practice the things I can teach her, and saving tiny coins when I can. I worry about the future — I want my daughter to go to school and learn to read, to have choices I never had. I want a more secure roof over our heads and a way to get to the clinic without counting and recounting cedis.

Community ties keep me going. When someone is in trouble we share food and labor. When the harvest is good, neighbors come together to celebrate. When it isn’t, we sit and plan. I try to be hopeful. Every time I see a health worker at a community meeting or hear of a job in town, I think of small steps forward. I may not have had a classroom, but I have learned resilience, care and how to stretch what little we have. Those are the lessons I pass on to my daughter as we walk the dusty path of Kwadia together.

We spend about 100 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food. That covers staples like gari, rice, plantain, garden vegetables, and some occasional meat when we can afford it. You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in Mokwa, a small community in the Twifo Atti Morkwa District in the Central Region, and I still live here at twenty-four. My earliest memories are of narrow dirt paths, mango trees that shaded the compound, and the steady hum of people going about their day. Our village only has about 1,176 people, so faces are familiar and news travels fast. I finished JSS — junior high school — but that was as far as formal education went for me. After JSS I started helping my parents and taking on odd jobs; school fees and the need to contribute at home meant I couldn’t continue.

There are six other people living in the house with me right now: my parents, two younger siblings, my younger cousin and his child — the one child under eighteen in the house. I’m the oldest and, over the last few years, I’ve been the main breadwinner. I work full time at a small general store and also run a little side supply to local markets a few mornings a week. The shop isn’t glamorous, but it keeps us afloat. On average we spend around 320 Ghanaian Cedis a week on food for the household and about 40 cedis on non-food items like water, electricity, and small school expenses. I wouldn’t say we’re rich — I rate our finances as neither good nor bad — but there’s stability, and that feels important.

One thing that has helped is our proximity to basic services. The nearest health clinic is almost next door — only about a hundred meters away — which made decisions about health care easier for us. When the COVID-19 vaccines became available, I felt it was the right thing to do; I understood the risk, I work with customers every day, and the clinic’s close. I was almost certain — I’d say ninety-seven percent — that I would take the first shot as soon as it was available. Having a clinic you can walk to changes your view on those things.

Family ties extend beyond our compound. I have seven family members living in another village and about fifteen friends and acquaintances who do the same. Locally I can name roughly ten people who make up my close social network — neighbours, cousins, and old classmates — and we rely on one another: sharing labor during harvest, pooling money when someone needs medicine, or watching each other’s houses during festivals. I don’t use social media; I prefer to stay connected the old way — through visits, calls, and being there in person. I do have a registered mobile number, though, and use it for calls and messages when I need to coordinate with suppliers or check on family.

My day starts early. I open the shop before sunrise, sweep, put items on the shelves, and greet whoever walks in — farmers, students, the clinic staff on their breaks. By mid-morning I may load a small order for the market or deliver supplies to a neighboring village where some of my customers live. Afternoons are for balancing accounts, talking with suppliers, and helping at home. Evenings are when the family sits together and plans — who needs extra support this week, which bills must be paid, and how we’ll manage if the yam harvest is late. I take pride in being dependable; my siblings look up to me, and I try to set an example even though my education ended at JSS.

I remember the day I filled out the interview form back in February 2022. I was a little nervous about the questions, but I answered honestly. The data captured things I already knew — how many people we are, how much we spend, who I talk to. But it also reminded me of how connected and interdependent life here is. Whether it’s walking a neighbour to the clinic, lending a small sum to a cousin in another village, or simply sharing a meal with people under the same roof, my life has been built around relationships and responsibilities.

Looking ahead, I’d like to expand the shop or partner with a few other young men from the village to start a transport run to the district capital on market days. That would help increase our income and make the household feel more secure. For now, I keep doing what I can: steady work, careful budgeting, being available for my family, and showing up for my community. That’s how I’ve come to define myself — a son, an older brother, a worker, and someone who keeps his promises.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I was born and raised in Dansame, a small but busy community in the Assin North District of the Central Region. I’m 24 now, and when I think about how my days are shaped, I always come back to the people under our roof and the work that keeps food on the table. Our village is about 4,620 people strong — everyone knows each other in one way or another — and I grew up learning to lean on neighbors and family. Even now I live in a large, crowded house: nine people live with me besides myself, and there are five children under 18 who I help care for every day. They’re my younger siblings and cousins more than my own children, but I take that responsibility seriously.

School stopped for me after JSS/JHS. I wanted to keep learning, but the family needed hands at home, and I had to find a way to help. I got my first steady job a couple of years after that, and on the morning of 2022-02-18 at 7:00 I walked into my new place of work for the first time, nervous and proud. That morning sticks with me — I remember the smell of the food market on the way, the careful counting of coins, and the tight feeling in my chest thinking about the bills waiting at home. My job is full-time; I work in a small retail shop in the trading center a short walk from the main road. I sell daily goods, take mobile money payments, and manage stock. It isn’t glamorous, but it pays the bills, and it has given me a steady income to support my household.

Money moves quickly in our house. We spend around 300 Ghana cedis a week on food — rice, gari, plantain, garri, cassava, fresh fish when we can, palm oil, vegetables — and about 100 cedis a week on non-food items like electricity, water, and school fees for the younger ones. Most weeks feel like balancing a tight rope: deciding whether to save a little or buy something extra for the children. I’d describe our household’s financial condition as neither good nor bad — we are stable enough to get by, but any unexpected cost, like a fever or a broken stove, quickly makes things difficult.

Health is always on my mind. The nearest health clinic is about 3.07 kilometers from where I live. It’s not too far, but when a child is sick or someone needs medication, the walk or the transport cost matters. I try to plan trips carefully, and I keep a little aside so that if we need to go, we can go without waiting. I’m not against modern medicine — I think about the COVID-19 vaccine a lot. If it was offered to me tomorrow, there’s a good chance I would get the first shot in the first six weeks — I’d say maybe a 70% chance. Part of me worries about side effects; part of me wants to protect the children and the older people in the compound. In the end I think I’d go, especially if the clinic staff we trust encouraged it.

Technology and people keep me connected. I have a registered mobile number and I check social media a few times every day. It helps me keep in touch with friends, sell a few things online now and then, and follow news about crop prices or the clinic. My social circle is big enough that I’m never lonely: I can name about 26 people right here in and around town I’d call friends or close relatives, and I also have family in another village — there are seven of them — plus six friends and acquaintances who live elsewhere. When there’s a wedding, funeral, or even a market day, we make plans together across villages.

My mornings are early. I wake before dawn, start the charcoal or fire to cook for everyone, sweep the compound, and get the younger ones ready for school. Then I head to the shop. The work is hands-on: serving customers, doing mobile money, managing small stock orders, and sometimes running errands. Evenings are for homework help, cooking, and talking with the older women in the house about what the next week will cost. Weekends I try to rest, visit relatives in nearby villages, or catch up on social media messages and save up any small profits I can to put toward school fees or a rainy-day fund.

I don’t have big degrees, but I’ve learned a lot through doing. I know how to stretch small amounts of money, how to read people when they try to haggle, and how to organize a household of ten so everyone gets something to eat. I am proud of that. I worry about the future sometimes — about more schooling, about saving enough to move into a smaller household so the children can have more space — but I wake up and do the work. This is my life in Dansame: rooted in family, shaped by a steady job, and connected to a network of friends and relatives who help carry the burdens and share the joys.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in a small but bustling community called JAMRA, in the Asikuma Odoben Brakwa District of the Central Region. I am 26 now, and when people ask where I went to school I tell them honestly that my formal education stopped after JSS — I finished junior high and then life pulled me in different directions. My family needed help at home, and opportunities to continue were limited, so I returned to the village and learned the practical things that keep a household and a small farm running.

My day begins early. I live in a house with five other people besides me — my husband, our three children (they are all under 18), and my mother-in-law. The house is full of noise and warmth. With three children, the mornings can be chaotic: preparing breakfast, getting small clothes ready for school, and making sure everyone has water to drink. I am a homemaker, and that role occupies most of my time. I cook, clean, look after the children, care for the small garden near the house, and manage the household money. My husband does occasional work on nearby farms and sometimes takes odd jobs in town when he can.

Money is always something we think about, but we are doing alright. On a typical week we spend about 150 Ghanaian Cedis on food — that covers the staples, fish, tomatoes, oil, and the occasional treat for the children. Non-food expenses like electricity, water, rent if any, and school-related costs amount to around 30 cedis a week. For us, that allows a life I would rate as good. We can pay for the basics, the children are in school, and there is food on the table most days. It is not a life of luxury, but it is steady, and I am grateful for it.

JAMRA is home to roughly 4,995 people. It is small enough that everyone knows each other, and there is a real sense of community. Neighbours help one another when crops fail or when a child is sick, and social gatherings and church bring people together. But part of living here is recognizing the limits of what the village can provide. The nearest health clinic is not very close — it is 6.35290709 kilometers away. That distance matters. When a child has a fever or needs immunization, the trip to the clinic takes time and costs transport money. For small ailments we often rely on home remedies and advice from older women in the community; for anything more serious we find a way to get to the clinic or a bigger hospital in town.

I have a registered mobile number, and my phone is a lifeline. I use it to call my husband, to get messages from relatives, to follow news, and sometimes to receive money through mobile transfers. It helps me stay connected and informed, though not everything I hear is easy to sort through. That plays into how I think about health decisions, including vaccines.

When the topic of COVID-19 vaccination comes up, I feel conflicted — about fifty-fifty, I would say. If the vaccine were available to me right now, I estimate a 49% chance I would get the first shot within the first six weeks. Part of me wants the protection it might give my children and myself; part of me worries about side effects and whether the vaccine is safe. I have heard mixed stories: some people say it is a shield, others whisper about problems. Practical considerations also matter — who will look after the children if I feel unwell after a dose? How will I travel to the clinic that is over six kilometers away? And will the clinic have the vaccine at all, or will I need to wait and come back again?

Still, I keep listening and learning. I talk to the nurse when she visits, I ask neighbours about their experiences, and I watch for reliable information on the radio and from community meetings. My hope is to make the right choice for my family: to protect them while also ensuring I can continue to care for my children without interruption. For now I keep preparing the house, tending the garden, and balancing the weekly budget, taking one day at a time in JAMRA, where life is simple but full.

You are also asked to provide a detailed backstory about yourself, which is provided below:
I grew up in Nkukuasa, a small close-knit community in the Assin North District of the Central Region. Our village has about fourteen hundred and sixty-five people — everyone knows everyone, and there is a safety in that familiarity. I finished JSS/JHS, and I still remember the crowded classroom, the chalk dust, and the way we shared textbooks. I had dreams of continuing my education, but life in our household required that I help out in other ways instead.

I am eighteen now. At the moment I am unemployed, but that doesn’t mean I’m idle. My days are full of small, steady tasks: helping my mother with cooking and market runs, tending a little plot of vegetables near the house, and looking after my younger brother. We are three people in the house — me, my mother, and my brother — and we depend on a mix of farming, small trading, and occasional support from relatives working in town. Our household spends about 140 cedis a week on food and roughly 80 cedis on non-food items like electricity, water, and other bills. That budget isn’t extravagant, but we manage, and I would describe our household condition as good. There’s a roof over our heads, food on the table, and enough left to pay the bills most weeks, so I feel grateful.

Living in a small community has its comforts and limits. We share news at the market, celebrate harvests together, and the children play until dusk. But services — especially health services — are not close. The nearest health clinic is just under twelve kilometers away, and when someone is sick that distance becomes real and heavy. We don’t always have reliable transport; sometimes we walk, sometimes we hire a motorbike. Because of that distance, I pay extra attention to our family’s health. That is partly why I am almost certain — about 92% sure — that I would take the first COVID-19 vaccine shot within the first six weeks it was available to me. I have seen illness change lives here, and if there is something that can protect us and keep my mother and brother safe, I want to take it.

One frustrating practical barrier in my life is that I don’t have a registered mobile number to receive payments. I use a neighbor’s phone or my mother’s phone when I need to make a call or check messages, but not having my own SIM and mobile money account limits my opportunities. When small paid tasks are posted or when people send money from town, I can’t receive it directly. I’d like to register a number and a mobile money account soon — it would make finding and accepting work, or receiving remittances from relatives, so much easier.

I answered these questions on 16 February 2022, and I remember thinking about how small details — the distance to the clinic, whether I have a phone number, the amount we spend each week — are parts of a bigger picture of my life. I would like to continue my education or get vocational training in something practical that can bring steady income: maybe tailoring, agro-processing, or working with digital services if I can sort out my mobile money access. For now I keep learning at home, helping my family, and keeping an eye on opportunities in our district center and the nearby towns.

The rhythm of life here is simple but full. I wake early to help with chores, walk to the market when we need supplies, laugh with neighbors over common worries, and think often about the future. My community’s closeness gives me strength, and the small comforts we have make me hopeful that with a little more support — a registered phone number, a training course, or a steady job — I can build something more for myself and help my family even more.
